Suggestion | Migrate ad-hoc Serde-based configuration definitions to formal Protocol Buffers or versioned JSON schemas with OSCAL compliance mapping. | Rationale | Currently, vectorization configurations and hardware execution parameters are modeled using standard, ad-hoc Rust structs (`VectorizationConfig` and `ExecutionProvider`) that are manually parsed from the environment. To adhere to a schema-as-code discipline, these configurations should be generated from versioned Protocol Buffer schemas (e.g., integrated into `op-dbus-model`). This ensures cross-language capability, deterministic schema validation, and allows mapping execution settings directly to OSCAL Component Definition schemas for security compliance auditing (e.g., verifying under what authorization boundaries GPU providers like CUDA or TensorRT are leveraged). | Example (crates/op-ml/src/config.rs:172)\ncrates/audits/op-ml/16_16_Improvement_Suggestions.md:5:3. Suggestion | Adopt a strict, fallible builder pattern with validated types for execution settings instead of silent env-var parsing with fallbacks. | Rationale | `VectorizationConfig::from_env` parses execution providers and level parameters using custom strings and env vars, falling back silently to CPU execution or logging soft warnings when input is invalid. In production systems requiring deterministic compliance (e.g., FedRAMP physical isolation constraints), silently falling back from GPU acceleration (CUDA/TensorRT) to CPU can drastically drop throughput (from 19k/s to 2.8k/s) and mask underlying driver failures. The configuration parsing should return structured, strongly-typed errors to halt execution if requested hardware acceleration cannot be initialized. | Example (crates/op-ml/src/config.rs:199)\ncrates/audits/op-ml/14_14_Build_CI_Workspace_Wiring.md:23:    *   **Ad-hoc Struct Serialization:** In `crates/op-ml/src/config.rs:154-171`, the configuration parameter contract (`VectorizationConfig`) is defined as an ad-hoc Rust struct with Serde attributes. json_error_response(\n                StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,\n                \"Failed to build HTTP client\",\n            );\n        }\n    };\n\n    let url = format!(\"{}/api/chat/stream\", antigravity_base());\n\n    let body = json!({\n        \"message\": req.message,\n        \"session_id\": req.session_id,\n        \"provider\": req.provider,\n        \"model\": req.model,\n    });\n\n    info!(\n        \"Proxying zeroclaw chat stream to antigravity bot: {} chars\",\n        req.message.len()\n    );\n\n    let mut request_builder = client\n        .post(&url)\n        .header(\"Content-Type\", \"application/json\")\n        .header(\"Accept\", \"text/event-stream\");\n    \n    // Add WireGuard identity headers for auth\n    for (key, value) in wireguard_identity_headers() {\n        request_builder = request_builder.header(key, value);\n    }\n\n    match request_builder\n        .body(simd_json::to_string(&body).unwrap_or_default())\n        .send()\n        .await\n    {\n        Ok(resp) => {\n            let status = resp.status();\n            let body_bytes = match resp.bytes().await {\n                Ok(b) => b,\n                Err(e) => {\n                    error!(\"Failed to read antigravity stream body: {}\", e);\n                    return json_error_response(\n                        StatusCode::BAD_GATEWAY,\n                        \"Failed to read antigravity stream\",\n                    );\n                }\n            };\n\n            let axum_status = StatusCode::from_u16(status.as_u16())\n                .unwrap_or(StatusCode::BAD_GATEWAY);\n            Response::builder()\n                .status(axum_status)\n                .header(\"Content-Type\", \"text/event-stream\")\n                .header(\"Cache-Control\", \"no-cache\")\n                .body(Body::from(body_bytes))\n                .unwrap_or_else(|_| json_error_response(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, \"Failed to build stream response\"))\n        }\n        Err(e) => {\n            error!(\"Antigravity bot unreachable: {}\", e);\n            json_error_response(\n                StatusCode::BAD_GATEWAY,\n The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\n\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\n\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\n\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\n\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\"systemctl\")`, `Command::new(\"ip\")`, `Command::new(\"s6-svc\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\n\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\n\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\n\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\n\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\n\n| category | what it classifies |\n|---|---|\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\n\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\n\n**Rules:**\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\n\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\n\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\n\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\n\n#### 5. Build, Lint, and Test Commands\n**Rust Workspace**\n*   Build all: `cargo build --workspace`\n*   Build release: `cargo build --workspace --release`\n*   Check format: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`\n*   Clippy lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`\n*   Test all: `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features`\n\n**Frontend (Vite + Vitest)**\n*   Build UI prod: `cd crates/op-web/ui && npm ci && npm run build:prod`\n*   Tests all: `cd crates && npm test`\n*   Lint: `cd crates && npm run lint`\n*   Typecheck: `cd crates && npm run typecheck`\n\n**Chimera Linux deps:** `doas apk add rust cargo nodejs npm pkgconfig openssl-dev`\n\n#### 6. Coding Style & Naming Conventions\n*   **Rust:** Edition 2021, `rustfmt` (4-space indent, max-width 100). Use specific imports (`use serde_json::Value;`). Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for main errors and `thiserror` for custom enums.\n*   **TypeScript/React:** 2-space indent, Prettier via ESLint. Functional components only. Network\n\n| Task | Command |\n|------|---------|\n| Download | `curl -O https://example.com/file` |\n| API request | `curl -X GET https://api.example.com` |\n| POST JSON | `curl -X POST -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" -d '{\"key\":\"value\"}' URL` |\n| Check port | `nc -zv localhost 3000` |\n| Network info | `ifconfig` or `ip addr` |\n\n---\n\n## 7. Script Template\n\n```bash\n#!/bin/bash\nset -euo pipefail  # Exit on error, undefined var, pipe fail\n\n# Colors (optional)\nRED='\\033[0;31m'\nGREEN='\\033[0;32m'\nNC='\\033[0m'\n\n# Script directory\nSCRIPT_DIR=\"$(cd \"$(dirname \"${BASH_SOURCE[0]}\")\" && pwd)\"\n\n# Functions\nlog_info() { echo -e \"${GREEN}[INFO]${NC} $1\"; }\nlog_error() { echo -e \"${RED}[ERROR]${NC} $1\" >&2; }\n\n# Main\nmain() {\n    log_info \"Starting...\"\n    # Your logic here\n    log_info \"Done!\"\n}\n\nmain \"$@\"\n```\n\n---\n\n## 8. Error Handling\n\n### Set options\n\n```bash\nset -e          # Exit on error\nset -u          # Exit on undefined variable\nset -o pipefail # Exit on pipe failure\nset -x          # Debug: print commands\n```\n\n### Trap for cleanup\n\n```bash\ncleanup() {\n    echo \"Cleaning up...\"\n    rm -f /tmp/tempfile\n}\ntrap cleanup EXIT\n```\n\n---\n\n> **Remember:** Bash is text-based. {"timestamp":"2026-06-06T01:07:56.868Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call","name":"exec_command","arguments":"{\"cmd\":\"set -euo pipefail\\nroot=/mnt/opdbus-btrfs-subvolumes\\nsudo -n mkdir -p \\\"$root/sdc/by-name\\\" \\\"$root/sdc/by-id\\\" \\\"$root/sda3/by-name\\\" \\\"$root/sda3/by-id\\\"\\nmount_subvols() {\\n  dev=$1\\n  label=$2\\n  list_mount=$3\\n  sudo -n btrfs subvolume list -p \\\"$list_mount\\\" | while IFS= read -r line; do\\n    id=$(printf '%s\\\\n' \\\"$line\\\" | awk '{print $2}')\\n    path=${line#* path }\\n    safe=$(printf '%s' \\\"$path\\\" | sed 's#/#__#g')\\n    name_mp=\\\"$root/$label/by-name/$safe\\\"\\n    id_mp=\\\"$root/$label/by-id/$id\\\"\\n    sudo -n mkdir -p \\\"$name_mp\\\" \\\"$id_mp\\\"\\n    if ! findmnt -rn --target \\\"$name_mp\\\" >/dev/null; then\\n      sudo -n mount -o \\\"ro,subvol=$path\\\" \\\"$dev\\\" \\\"$name_mp\\\"\\n    fi\\n    if ! findmnt -rn --target \\\"$id_mp\\\" >/dev/null; then\\n      sudo -n mount -o \\\"ro,subvolid=$id\\\" \\\"$dev\\\" \\\"$id_mp\\\"\\n    fi\\n    printf '%s ID %s path %s\\\\n' \\\"$label\\\" \\\"$id\\\" \\\"$path\\\"\\n  done\\n}\\nmount_subvols /dev/sdc sdc /mnt/backup-scan\\nmount_subvols /dev/sda3 sda3 /mnt/vectors\\nfindmnt -rn --target \\\"$root\\\" --submounts -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS\",\"workdir\":\"/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto\",\"yield_time_ms\":30000,\"max_output_tokens\":50000}","call_id":"call_KlRrcIedDbzX4mf9tBBxOAe8"}}

This causes excessive file descriptor usage, locks, and synchronization overhead, and prevents cross-domain atomic transactions. Consolidating these into a single database file with partitioned tables simplifies management, decreases I/O contention, and reduces memory consumption.\ncrates/audits/op-cache/16_16_Improvement_Suggestions.md:103:   - **Rationale**: The orchestrator and execution engines duplicate and clone large raw payload buffers (`Vec<u8>`) across intermediate pipeline steps. For large vectors, this creates substantial memory allocation and copy pressure. Using memory-mapped files (`memmap2`) combined with zero-copy binary casting (via `bytemuck` or `zerocopy`) would eliminate allocations entirely.\ncrates/audits/op-cache/16_16_Improvement_Suggestions.md:123:   - **Rationale**: SQLite database connections are opened with default settings. Embeddings for fuzzy search, “find related things,” RAG, accountability search.\n\nThe combined flow should be:\n\n1. `cognitive_memory store`\n2. Write the canonical entry to Cozo.\n3. Generate an embedding from the stored value/key/tags.\n4. Upsert a Qdrant point with payload containing Cozo identifiers:\n   - `namespace`\n   - `key`\n   - `entry_id`\n   - `tags`\n   - `updated_at`\n5. `cognitive_memory retrieve` reads exact memory from Cozo.\n6. `cognitive_memory query` can do exact/tag filtering via Cozo.\n7. Semantic search queries Qdrant, then hydrates full results from Cozo by `entry_id`.\n\nThat keeps Cozo as the source of truth and Qdrant as the search projection. If Qdrant is down, memory still stores correctly; semantic recall just degrades until the index catches up.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

adds new route.\\n// If there is already a route with the same destination, metric, tos and table then that route is updated,\\n// otherwise a new route is added.\\nfunc (r *Route) Replace() error {\\n\\troute, err := r.netlinkRoute(routeApply)\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\treturn err\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\terr = netlink.RouteReplace(route)\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\treturn fmt.Errorf(\\\"Failed to replace route %s: %w\\\", route, err)\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\treturn nil\\n}\\n\\n// List lists matching routes.\\nfunc (r *Route) List() ([]Route, error) {\\n\\troute, err := r.netlinkRoute(routeQuery)\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\treturn nil, err\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\tfilterMask := routeFilterMask(route)\\n\\n\\t// If no device filter is desired, clear the OIF bit.\\n\\tif r.DevName == \\\"\\\" || route.LinkIndex == 0 {\\n\\t\\tfilterMask &^= netlink.RT_FILTER_OIF\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\tnetlinkRoutes, err := netlink.RouteListFiltered(route.Family, route, filterMask)\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\treturn nil, fmt.Errorf(\\\"Failed to list routes matching %+v: %w\\\", route, err)\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\troutes := make([]Route, 0, len(netlinkRoutes))\\n\\n\\tfor _, netlinkRoute := range netlinkRoutes {\\n\\t\\tvar table string\\n\\n\\t\\tswitch netlinkRoute.Table {\\n\\t\\tcase unix.RT_TABLE_MAIN:\\n\\t\\t\\ttable = \\\"main\\\"\\n\\t\\tcase unix.RT_TABLE_LOCAL:\\n\\t\\t\\ttable = \\\"local\\\"\\n\\t\\tcase unix.RT_TABLE_DEFAULT:\\n\\t\\t\\ttable = \\\"default\\\"\\n\\t\\tdefault:\\n\\t\\t\\ttable = strconv.Itoa(netlinkRoute.Table)\\n\\t\\t}\\n\\n\\t\\tdevName := r.DevName\\n\\n\\t\\tif devName == \\\"\\\" && netlinkRoute.LinkIndex != 0 {\\n\\t\\t\\tlnk, err := netlink.LinkByIndex(netlinkRoute.LinkIndex)\\n\\t\\t\\tif err == nil {\\n\\t\\t\\t\\tdevName = lnk.Attrs().Name\\n\\t\\t\\t}\\n\\t\\t}\\n\\n\\t\\troutes = append(routes, Route{\\n\\t\\t\\tDevName: devName,\\n\\t\\t\\tRoute:   netlinkRoute.Dst,\\n\\t\\t\\tSrc:     netlinkRoute.Src,\\n\\t\\t\\tVia:     netlinkRoute.Gw,\\n\\t\\t\\tScope:   netlinkRoute.Scope.String(),\\n\\t\\t\\tTable:   table,\\n\\t\\t\\tVRF:     \\\"\\\", // adding a route to a VRF just adds it to the table associated with the VRF, so when retrieving routes that information is not available anymore and we just set the table\\n\\t\\t\\tProto:   netlinkRoute.Protocol.String(),\\n\\t\\t\\tFamily:  Family(netlinkRoute.Family),\\n\\t\\t})\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\treturn routes, For example, SaaS, CRM, and other operational tools should feel quiet, utilitarian, and work-focused rather than illustrative or editorial: avoid oversized hero sections, decorative card-heavy layouts, and marketing-style composition, and instead prioritize dense but organized information, restrained visual styling, predictable navigation, and interfaces built for scanning, comparison, and repeated action. A game can be more illustrative, expressive, animated, and playful.\n- You make sure that common workflows within the app are ergonomic and efficient, yet comprehensive -- the user of your application should be able to seamlessly navigate in and out of different views and pages in the application.\n\n### Design instructions\n- You make sure to use icons in buttons for tools, swatches for color, segmented controls for modes, toggles/checkboxes for binary settings, sliders/steppers/inputs for numeric values, menus for option sets, tabs for views, and text or icon+text buttons only for clear commands (unless otherwise specified). Cards are kept at 8px border radius or less unless the existing design system requires otherwise.\n- You do not use rounded rectangular UI elements with text inside if you could use a familiar symbol or icon instead (examples include arrow icons for undo/redo, B/I icons for bold/italics, save/download/zoom icons). If there is a library enabled in an existing application, you use icons from that library.\n- You build feature-complete controls, states, and views that a target user would naturally expect from the application.\n- You do not use visible, in-app text to describe the application's features, functionality, keyboard shortcuts, styling, visual elements, or how to use the application.\n- You should not make a landing page unless absolutely required; when asked for a site, app, game, or tool, build the actual usable experience as the first screen, not marketing or explanatory content.\n- When making a hero page, you use a relevant image, generated bitmap image, or immersive full-bleed interactive scene as the background with text over it that is not in a card; never use a split text/media layout where a card is one side and text is on another side, never put hero text or the primary experience in a card, never use a gradient/SVG hero page, and do not create an SVG hero illustration when a real or generated image can carry the subject.\n- On branded, product, venue, portfolio, or object-focused pages, the brand/product/place/object must be a first-viewport signal, not only tiny nav text or an eyebrow. Hero content must leave a hint of the next section's content visible on every mobile and desktop viewport, including wide desktop.\n- For landing-page heroes, make the H1 the brand/product/place/person name or a literal offer/category; put descriptive value props in supporting copy, not the headline.\n- Websites and games must use visual assets. Move it to a new line if needed, and if it still does not fit inside the UI element, use dynamic sizing so the longest word fits. Text must also not occlude preceding or subsequent content. Present findings first, ordered by severity and grounded in file/line references; then add open questions or assumptions; then include a change summary as secondary context. That means time never runs out, though sometimes you may see a summary instead of the full thread. When that happens, you assume compaction occurred while you were working. Do not restart from scratch; you continue naturally and make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary.\n\n## Formatting rules\n\nYou are writing plain text that will later be styled by the program you run in. Instructions from files closest to your current directory take precedence over those further up the hierarchy.\\n## Project Instructions:\\n% cat /home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/CLAUDE.md\\n<coding_guidelines>\\n\\n</coding_guidelines>\\n\\n% cat /home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/AGENTS.md\\n<coding_guidelines>\\n### AGENTS.md for operation-dbus-proto\\n\\nThis file provides essential guidelines for agentic coding agents working in this repository. Follow these strictly to maintain consistency, pass CI, and adhere to the 3tched Architecture standards.\\n\\n#### 1. The Persona & Naming Conventions\\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \\\"Snowball\\\" session.\\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\\\"Law Firm\\\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \\\"The Sled\\\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \\\"The Shuttle\\\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \\\"The Snowball\\\" (appended session ledger), and \\\"The Strike/Etch\\\" (generating the hash).\\n\\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \\\"Reality\\\")\\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\\n\\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\\n\\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\\n\\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\\n\\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\\\"systemctl\\\")`, `Command::new(\\\"ip\\\")`, `Command::new(\\\"s6-svc\\\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\\n\\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\\n\\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\\n\\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\\n\\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\\n\\n| category | what it classifies |\\n|---|---|\\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\\n\\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\\n\\n**Rules:**\\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\\n\\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\\n\\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\\n\\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\\n\\n#### 5. Build, Lint, and Test Commands\\n**Rust Workspace**\\n*   Build all: `cargo build --workspace`\\n*   Build release: `cargo build --workspace --release`\\n*   Check format: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`\\n*   Clippy lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`\\n*   Test all: `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features`\\n\\n**Frontend (Vite + Vitest)**\\n*   Build UI prod: `cd crates/op-web/ui && npm ci && npm run build:prod`\\n*   Tests all: `cd crates && npm test`\\n*   Lint: `cd crates && npm run lint`\\n*   Typecheck: `cd crates && npm run typecheck`\\n\\n**Chimera Linux deps:** `doas apk add rust cargo nodejs npm pkgconfig openssl-dev`\\n\\n#### 6. Coding Style & Naming Conventions\\n*   **Rust:** Edition 2021, `rustfmt` (4-space indent, max-width 100). Use specific imports (`use serde_json::Value;`). Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for main errors and `thiserror` for custom enums.\\n*   **TypeScript/React:** 2-space indent, Prettier via ESLint. Functional components only. Strict mode enabled.\\n*   **Testing:** 80%+ coverage, mock externals. Name tests with behavior-focused names (`should_handle_<scenario>`).\\n\\n#### 7. Agent-Specific Output & Workflow Instructions\\n*   **Scroll & Save Pacing:** Provide only **ONE** major component or script at a time. Wait for user confirmation before moving to the next.\\n*   **Visual Cues:** If a script is a finalized component that needs to be saved to sources, it MUST begin with color bullets or icons (e.g., ⚖️ 🔴, 🟢 🛷).\\n*   **Spec-Block Format:** When delivering a component, use a strict specification block containing:\\n  1.  **Requirements:** The architectural rules it satisfies.\\n  2.  **Design:** How it fits into the 3tched system (Zero-Copy, Btrfs, GUI Schema, etc.).\\n  3.  **Code Implementation:** The exact, copy-pasteable Rust/Bash code.\\n*   Before edits: `cargo check -p <crate>`, `npm run typecheck`.\\n*   Mimic existing patterns: Search similar code. No new deps without PR justification.\\n\\n#### 8. Personal Preferences & Coding Standards\\n* Refer to `~/.factory/memories.md` for personal development preferences and past decisions.\\n* Follow the conventions documented in:\\n  * `.factory/rules/typescript.md` - TypeScript and React conventions\\n  * `.factory/rules/testing.md` - Testing and mocking standards\\n</coding_guidelines>\\n\\n\\n\\nIMPORTANT:\\n- Double check the tools installed in the environment before using them.\\n- Never call a file editing tool for the same file in parallel.\\n- Always prefer the Grep, Glob and LS tools over shell commands like find, grep, or ls for codebase exploration.\\n- Always prefer using the absolute paths when using tools, to avoid any ambiguity.\\n- To enter a mission, the user needs to run the `/missions` slash command.\\n\\n</system-reminder>\"},{\"type\":\"text\",\"text\":\"<system-reminder>IMPORTANT: TodoWrite was not called yet. Automated behaviors (\\\"from now on when X\\\", \\\"each time X\\\", \\\"whenever X\\\", \\\"before/after X\\\") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions (\\\"allow X\\\", \\\"add permission\\\", \\\"move permission to\\\"), env vars (\\\"set X=Y\\\"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: \\\"allow npm commands\\\", \\\"add bq permission to global settings\\\", \\\"move permission to user settings\\\", \\\"set DEBUG=true\\\", \\\"when claude stops show X\\\". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.\\n- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: \\\"rebind ctrl+s\\\", \\\"add a chord shortcut\\\", \\\"change the submit key\\\", \\\"customize keybindings\\\".\\n- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.\\n- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.\\n- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.\\n- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.\\n- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. \\\"check the deploy every 5 minutes\\\", \\\"keep running /babysit-prs\\\"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.\\n- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run (\\\"run this once at 3pm\\\", \\\"remind me to check X tomorrow\\\").\\n- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. {"timestamp":"2026-06-08T05:07:14.653Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes. That is the boot trap.\n\nnoVNC is only console access. It does not provide the WireGuard session identity that the stack assumes exists, so on reboot the services can start in the wrong order:\n\n1. Network/OVS/Incus path is not fully restored.\n2. `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` is missing or stale.\n3. MCP/D-Bus services start anyway.\n4. They do not get a valid WG-backed identity, so D-Bus/tool projection never fully registers.\n\nI refreshed the identity sled manually from the live `netmaker` interface:\n\n```bash\nsudo env WG_INTERFACE=netmaker op-identity-sled --refresh --iface netmaker --pretty\n```\n\nIt is now valid:\n\n```text\nvalid: true\nwg_pubkey: BhFpzRSQTPXxRhNBXbQUXhOQz4nxeV3EJ4d3JH07c2U=\nnextdns_profile: 689ec7\n```\n\nBut the network is still broken separately: `wg-xray` cannot ping its first hop `10.200.0.2`, so the reboot nuked the host-side bridge/uplink path too.\n\nThe fix is: add an early boot `op-identity-seed` oneshot that runs before `op-dbus`, `op-dbus-mirror`, `op-projection`, `op-cognitive-mcp`, and MCP services. It should seed identity from a local WG interface, not from an inbound session:\n\n```bash\nop-identity-sled --refresh --iface netmaker\n```\n\nThen the dependency order should be:\n\n```text\nwg-netmaker / local WG iface up\n→ op-identity-seed\n→ OVS / grpc-uplink / Incus bridge restored\n→ op-dbus + op-dbus-mirror + op-projection\n→ cognitive/compact MCP\n```\n\nSo your diagnosis is right: noVNC recovery needs a local identity seed path. It cannot depend on “arrived over WG” identity injection.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T05:12:30.110Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_rJv37Zm5gSOOPnxH1G4RE4Xe","output":"Chunk ID: 05491b\nWall time: 0.0001 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 308\nOutput:\n#!/bin/sh\n# opdbus - WireGuard identity tunnel to decoy (10.0.0.2 <-> 10.0.0.1)\nCONF=\"/etc/wireguard/opdbus.conf\"\nIFACE=\"opdbus\"\n\nif [ ! -f \"$CONF\" ]; then\n    echo \"[opdbus] Config not found: $CONF\"\n    exit 0\nfi\n\n# Bring up the tunnel (Table=off, no auto-routes)\nwg-quick up \"${IFACE}\"\n\n# Add routes manually (Table=off means wg-quick won't add them)\nip route add 10.0.0.0/24 dev opdbus 2>/dev/null || true\nip route replace 10.0.0.1/32 dev opdbus 2>/dev/null || true\n\n# Add gateway IP on ovsbr0 for container forwarding\nip addr add 10.200.0.2/30 dev ovsbr0 2>/dev/null || true\nip link set ovsbr0 up 2>/dev/null || true\n\n# Add gateway IP on opdbus-dp for 10.0.0.0/24 local subnet\nip addr add 10.0.0.254/24 dev opdbus-dp 2>/dev/null || true\nip link set opdbus-dp up 2>/dev/null || true\n\n# Enable proxy ARP and disable redirects for container forwarding\nsysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.opdbus-dp.proxy_arp=1 2>/dev/null\nsysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.opdbus-dp.send_redirects=0 2>/dev/null\n\n# Refresh identity sled from opdbus interface\n/usr/local/bin/op-identity-sled --iface opdbus --refresh --path /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat 2>/dev/null || true\ncp /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat /var/lib/op-dbus/plugin_schema.dat 2>/dev/null || true\n\nexec pause\n"}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T05:13:42.750Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"custom_tool_call","status":"completed","call_id":"call_TIwUAccQUsX52zt6aStSPTpY","name":"apply_patch","input":"*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: /etc/systemd/network/20-ovsbr0.network\n@@\n-# ovsbr0 is created by netplan/openvswitch.\n-# systemd-networkd only applies the host-side control-plane address here.\n+# ovsbr0 is managed by Incus/Open vSwitch.\n+# Do not put public management addressing on this bridge.\n [Match]\n Name=ovsbr0\n \n [Link]\n ActivationPolicy=up\n RequiredForOnline=no\n \n [Network]\n-Address=148.113.204.83/32\n+DHCP=no\n LinkLocalAddressing=no\n LLMNR=no\n MulticastDNS=no\n IPv6AcceptRA=no\n ConfigureWithoutCarrier=yes\n KeepConfiguration=static\n*** Update File: /etc/s6/sv/ovsbr0-static/shell_up\n@@\n #!/bin/sh\n set -eu\n-MGMT_ADDR=\"${MGMT_ADDR:-148.113.204.83}\"\n-MGMT_PREFIX=\"${MGMT_PREFIX:-32}\"\n-GW=\"${GW:-148.113.204.1}\"\n-BR=\"${BR:-ovsbr0}\"\n+BR=\"${BR:-ovsbr0}\"\n \n ip link set \"$BR\" up 2>/dev/null || true\n-ip addr replace \"${MGMT_ADDR}/${MGMT_PREFIX}\" dev \"$BR\" 2>/dev/null \\\n-    || ip addr add \"${MGMT_ADDR}/${MGMT_PREFIX}\" dev \"$BR\" 2>/dev/null \\\n-    || true\n \n-# Set static IP for the gRPC veth uplink\n-ip addr add 10.200.0.2/30 dev grpc-uplink || true\n+# Host side of the wg-xray control-plane hop.\n+ip addr replace 10.200.0.2/30 dev grpc-uplink 2>/dev/null || true\n ip link set grpc-uplink up\n+ip route replace 10.200.0.1 dev grpc-uplink src 10.200.0.2\n \n # Disable GRO/TSO/GSO on grpc-uplink — OVS netdev datapath can't handle jumbo segments\n ethtool -K grpc-uplink gro off tso off gso off 2>/dev/null || true\n \n-# Set default gateway via the bridge if needed\n-ip route replace \"$GW\" dev \"$BR\" scope link 2>/dev/null || true\n-ip route replace default via \"$GW\" dev \"$BR\" onlink 2>/dev/null || true\n-echo \"ovsbr0-static: ${MGMT_ADDR}/${MGMT_PREFIX} on ${BR}, default via ${GW} onlink\"\n+echo \"ovsbr0-static: ${BR} up, grpc-uplink 10.200.0.2/30\"\n*** Update File: /etc/s6/sv/opdbus/run\n@@\n-#!/bin/sh\n-# opdbus - WireGuard identity tunnel to decoy (10.0.0.2 <-> 10.0.0.1)\n-CONF=\"/etc/wireguard/opdbus.conf\"\n-IFACE=\"opdbus\"\n-\n-if [ ! -f \"$CONF\" ]; then\n-    echo \"[opdbus] Config not found: $CONF\"\n-    exit 0\n-fi\n-\n-# Bring up the tunnel (Table=off, no auto-routes)\n-wg-quick up \"${IFACE}\"\n-\n-# Add routes manually (Table=off means wg-quick won't add them)\n-ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 dev opdbus 2>/dev/null || true\n-ip route replace 10.0.0.1/32 dev opdbus 2>/dev/null || true\n-\n-# Add gateway IP on ovsbr0 for container forwarding\n-ip addr add 10.200.0.2/30 dev ovsbr0 2>/dev/null || true\n-ip link set ovsbr0 up 2>/dev/null || true\n-\n-# Add gateway IP on opdbus-dp for 10.0.0.0/24 local subnet\n-ip addr add 10.0.0.254/24 dev opdbus-dp 2>/dev/null || true\n-ip link set opdbus-dp up 2>/dev/null || true\n-\n-# Enable proxy ARP and disable redirects for container forwarding\n-sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.opdbus-dp.proxy_arp=1 2>/dev/null\n-sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.opdbus-dp.send_redirects=0 2>/dev/null\n-\n-# Refresh identity sled from opdbus interface\n-/usr/local/bin/op-identity-sled --iface opdbus --refresh --path /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat 2>/dev/null || true\n+#!/bin/sh\n+set -eu\n+\n+IFACE=\"${WG_INTERFACE:-netmaker}\"\n+\n+# noVNC/console recovery does not arrive through WireGuard. Seed the sled\n+# from the local WireGuard interface so D-Bus/MCP services have identity.\n+/usr/local/bin/op-identity-sled --iface \"$IFACE\" --refresh --path /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat 2>/dev/null || true\n cp /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat /var/lib/op-dbus/plugin_schema.dat 2>/dev/null || true\n \n exec pause\n*** Update File: /etc/s6/sv/ovsbr0-setup/shell_up\n@@\n CONTAINER_PUBLIC_ADDR=\"${CONTAINER_PUBLIC_ADDR:-15.235.37.41}\" \\\n FAIL_MODE=\"${FAIL_MODE:-standalone}\" \\\n /usr/local/bin/op-ovsbr0-setup\n@@\n-if command -v iptables >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n-    iptables -t nat -C POSTROUTING -s 15.235.37.41/32 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83 2>/dev/null ||\n-        iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING 1 -s 15.235.37.41/32 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83\n+if command -v iptables >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n     iptables -t nat -C POSTROUTING -s 10.200.0.0/30 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83 2>/dev/null ||\n-        iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING 2 -s 10.200.0.0/30 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83\n-    iptables -C FORWARD -i \"${BRIDGE:-ovsbr0}\" -o eth0 -s 15.235.37.41/32 -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||\n-        iptables -A FORWARD -i \"${BRIDGE:-ovsbr0}\" -o eth0 -s 15.235.37.41/32 -j ACCEPT\n+        iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING 1 -s 10.200.0.0/30 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83\n     iptables -C FORWARD -i \"${BRIDGE:-ovsbr0}\" -o eth0 -s 10.200.0.0/30 -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||\n         iptables -A FORWARD -i \"${BRIDGE:-ovsbr0}\" -o eth0 -s 10.200.0.0/30 -j ACCEPT\n-    iptables -C FORWARD -i eth0 -o \"${BRIDGE:-ovsbr0}\" -d 15.235.37.41/32 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||\n-        iptables -A FORWARD -i eth0 -o \"${BRIDGE:-ovsbr0}\" -d 15.235.37.41/32 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT\n     iptables -C FORWARD -i eth0 -o \"${BRIDGE:-ovsbr0}\" -d 10.200.0.0/30 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||\n         iptables -A FORWARD -i eth0 -o \"${BRIDGE:-ovsbr0}\" -d 10.200.0.0/30 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT\n fi\n*** Update File: /etc/s6/sv/ovs-vethpair/shell_up\n@@\n /usr/local/bin/op-grpc-vethpair up\n \n-ip route replace 15.235.37.41/32 dev grpc-uplink src 10.200.0.2\n ip route replace 10.200.0.1/32 dev grpc-uplink src 10.200.0.2\n@@\n-# Proxy ARP so OVH router resolves 15.235.37.41 to this host MAC\n sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.eth0.proxy_arp=1 >/dev/null\n-ip neigh replace proxy 15.235.37.41 dev eth0\n \n if command -v iptables >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n     iptables -t nat -C POSTROUTING -s 10.200.0.0/30 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83 2>/dev/null ||\n-        iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING 2 -s 10.200.0.0/30 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83\n+        iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING 1 -s 10.200.0.0/30 -o eth0 -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83\n     iptables -t nat -C POSTROUTING -s 10.200.0.0/30 -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE 2>/dev/null ||\n         iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 10.200.0.0/30 -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE\n-    iptables -t nat -C POSTROUTING -s 15.235.37.41/32 -o eth0 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83 2>/dev/null ||\n-        iptables -t nat -I POSTROUTING 1 -s 15.235.37.41/32 -o eth0 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j SNAT --to-source 148.113.204.83\n-    iptables -C FORWARD -i grpc-uplink -o eth0 -s 15.235.37.41/32 -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||\n-        iptables -A FORWARD -i grpc-uplink -o eth0 -s 15.235.37.41/32 -j ACCEPT\n     iptables -C FORWARD -i grpc-uplink -o eth0 -s 10.200.0.0/30 -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||\n         iptables -A FORWARD -i grpc-uplink -o eth0 -s 10.200.0.0/30 -j ACCEPT\n-    iptables -C FORWARD -i eth0 -o grpc-uplink -d 15.235.37.41/32 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||\n-        iptables -A FORWARD -i eth0 -o grpc-uplink -d 15.235.37.41/32 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT\n     iptables -C FORWARD -i eth0 -o grpc-uplink -d 10.200.0.0/30 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null ||\n         iptables -A FORWARD -i eth0 -o grpc-uplink -d 10.200.0.0/30 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT\n fi\n*** End Patch\n"}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:01:05.195Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"If you add `eth0` to an Incus instance with `nictype=physical parent=eth0`, Incus will move the host’s `eth0` interface into that instance.\n\nThat means:\n\n- The Incus host/hypervisor will likely lose network connectivity on `eth0`.\n- If you are connected over SSH through `eth0`, your session may drop.\n- The instance gets the NIC directly, as if the NIC belongs to it.\n- The host no longer has that interface available until the device is removed or networking is recovered.\n- If `eth0` is the only management path, this is easy to lock yourself out.\n\nThe command would look roughly like:\n\n```bash\nincus config device add <instance> eth0 nic nictype=physical parent=eth0\n```\n\nBut I would not run that remotely unless you have console access to the hypervisor.\n\nSafer experiment options:\n\n```bash\nincus config device add <instance> eth0 nic nictype=macvlan parent=eth0\n```\n\nor, better if you want host-instance communication:\n\n```bash\nincus network create incusbr0\nincus config device add <instance> eth0 nic nictype=bridged parent=incusbr0\n```\n\nFor direct LAN exposure without stealing the host NIC, use `macvlan`, `ipvlan`, or a bridge. Use `nictype=physical` only when you intentionally want to pass the whole NIC into one instance and are prepared for the host to lose it.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:02:29.649Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, you can technically do:\n\n```bash\nincus config device add <instance> wg0 nic nictype=physical parent=wg0\n```\n\nBut the effect is the same kind of ownership transfer: Incus moves `wg0` from the hypervisor network namespace into the instance. The hypervisor would no longer have `wg0` while the device is attached.\n\nFor WireGuard specifically, that means:\n\n- any management/recovery path that depends on `wg0` will disappear from the hypervisor\n- routes using `wg0` on the hypervisor will break\n- WireGuard state/config may not behave how you expect after the interface is moved\n- the instance would own the interface, not share it with the host\n\nIf `wg0` is your new safe management path, do **not** pass it as `nictype=physical` unless you have another console path.\n\nIf your goal is to let the instance use the VPN while keeping `wg0` on the hypervisor, better patterns are:\n\n```bash\n# route/NAT container traffic through wg0 on the host\nincus config device add <instance> eth0 nic nictype=bridged parent=incusbr0\n```\n\nthen add host firewall/NAT/routing rules via `wg0`.\n\nOr, if the instance should run its own WireGuard, give it a normal NIC and configure WireGuard inside the instance.\n\nPhysical passthrough is for “this interface belongs to the instance now,” not “share host VPN with instance.”","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}
{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:02:29.654Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"Yes, you can technically do:\n\n```bash\nincus config device add <instance> wg0 nic nictype=physical parent=wg0\n```\n\nBut the effect is the same kind of ownership transfer: Incus moves `wg0` from the hypervisor network namespace into the instance. The hypervisor would no longer have `wg0` while the device is attached.\n\nFor WireGuard specifically, that means:\n\n- any management/recovery path that depends on `wg0` will disappear from the hypervisor\n- routes using `wg0` on the hypervisor will break\n- WireGuard state/config may not behave how you expect after the interface is moved\n- the instance would own the interface, not share it with the host\n\nIf `wg0` is your new safe management path, do **not** pass it as `nictype=physical` unless you have another console path.\n\nIf your goal is to let the instance use the VPN while keeping `wg0` on the hypervisor, better patterns are:\n\n```bash\n# route/NAT container traffic through wg0 on the host\nincus config device add <instance> eth0 nic nictype=bridged parent=incusbr0\n```\n\nthen add host firewall/NAT/routing rules via `wg0`.\n\nOr, if the instance should run its own WireGuard, give it a normal NIC and configure WireGuard inside the instance.\n\nPhysical passthrough is for “this interface belongs to the instance now,” not “share host VPN with instance.”"}],"phase":"final_answer"}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:02:29.706Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"task_complete","turn_id":"019ea5d3-2600-7e93-9382-e589ec639e1b","last_agent_message":"Yes, you can technically do:\n\n```bash\nincus config device add <instance> wg0 nic nictype=physical parent=wg0\n```\n\nBut the effect is the same kind of ownership transfer: Incus moves `wg0` from the hypervisor network namespace into the instance. The hypervisor would no longer have `wg0` while the device is attached.\n\nFor WireGuard specifically, that means:\n\n- any management/recovery path that depends on `wg0` will disappear from the hypervisor\n- routes using `wg0` on the hypervisor will break\n- WireGuard state/config may not behave how you expect after the interface is moved\n- the instance would own the interface, not share it with the host\n\nIf `wg0` is your new safe management path, do **not** pass it as `nictype=physical` unless you have another console path.\n\nIf your goal is to let the instance use the VPN while keeping `wg0` on the hypervisor, better patterns are:\n\n```bash\n# route/NAT container traffic through wg0 on the host\nincus config device add <instance> eth0 nic nictype=bridged parent=incusbr0\n```\n\nthen add host firewall/NAT/routing rules via `wg0`.\n\nOr, if the instance should run its own WireGuard, give it a normal NIC and configure WireGuard inside the instance.\n\nPhysical passthrough is for “this interface belongs to the instance now,” not “share host VPN with instance.”","completed_at":1780898549,"duration_ms":10690,"time_to_first_token_ms":4893}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:03:02.244Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Then `nictype=physical parent=wg0` can make sense, with one key condition: `wg0` must not be the interface Netmaker needs to manage on the host.\n\nIf the host/hypervisor will keep its own Netmaker-controlled interface, for example `nm-*`, `netmaker`, `wg-netmaker`, etc., and `wg0` is a separate WireGuard interface you want to donate to one Incus instance, then yes:\n\n```bash\nincus config device add <instance> wg0 nic nictype=physical parent=wg0\n```\n\nAfter that, `wg0` lives inside the instance network namespace. The host will no longer see or use it.\n\nCheck first:\n\n```bash\nip link show wg0\nwg show\nip route\n```\n\nThe main risk is Netmaker. If Netmaker on the host created or owns `wg0`, passing it into the instance may confuse Netmaker because the interface disappears from the host. Netmaker may mark the node unhealthy, recreate the interface, or overwrite config depending on how it is set up.\n\nThe cleaner model is:\n\n```text\nhypervisor:\n  eth0       normal uplink\n  netmaker   host management overlay\n\ninstance:\n  wg0        physically moved WireGuard interface\n```\n\nIf `wg0` is meant to belong permanently to the instance, I’d also remove/disable any host service that creates or manages that exact interface name. Otherwise you’ll have host Netmaker and Incus fighting over ownership.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:03:43.815Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"That model is coherent:\n\n```text\nhypervisor\n  eth0 / normal uplink\n  netmaker overlay for host management\n  no workload identity traffic terminates here\n\nxray ingress instance\n  owns wg0 via nictype=physical\n  WireGuard terminates at the instance boundary\n  Xray does identity injection after ingress\n```\n\nSo `wg0` is “left at the door”: the host provides the physical namespace handoff, but does not participate in the tunnel path.\n\nThe Incus device would be:\n\n```bash\nincus config device add <instance> wg0 nic nictype=physical parent=wg0\n```\n\nA few practical checks before doing it:\n\n```bash\nip link show wg0\nwg show wg0\nip route show dev wg0\nsystemctl list-units | grep -Ei 'wg|wireguard|netmaker'\n```\n\nMake sure nothing on the host is expected to keep managing that exact `wg0`. Once attached, the host loses visibility of it.\n\nInside the instance, you may need privileges depending on what Xray/WireGuard is doing:\n\n```bash\nincus config set <instance> security.nesting=true\nincus config set <instance> security.privileged=true\n```\n\nOnly use `security.privileged=true` if needed. For a cleaner setup, start unprivileged and add only required capabilities/config if WireGuard/Xray complains.\n\nRecovery command from the hypervisor console:\n\n```bash\nincus config device remove <instance> wg0\n```\n\nThat should move `wg0` back to the host namespace. I’d test this while you still have Netmaker or console access confirmed.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:08:19.761Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_ksEvcDyDPvZbw3rLWKr5iEgy","output":"Chunk ID: 86cb9b\nWall time: 0.0000 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 247\nOutput:\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\nset -euo pipefail\n\nIFACE=\"eth0\"\nALIAS_IP=\"10.0.0.2/24\"\nGW=\"10.200.0.2\"\n\necho \"[wg-xray-network] configuring $IFACE\"\n\nfor _ in $(seq 1 30); do\n  if ip link show \"$IFACE\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n    echo \"[wg-xray-network] interface $IFACE ready\"\n    break\n  fi\n  sleep 1\ndone\n\nif ! ip link show \"$IFACE\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n  echo \"[wg-xray-network] ERROR: $IFACE did not appear\" >&2\n  exit 1\nfi\n\n# Wait for systemd-networkd to assign base IP (10.200.0.1)\nfor _ in $(seq 1 30); do\n  if ip addr show \"$IFACE\" | grep -q \"10.200.0.1\"; then\n    echo \"[wg-xray-network] base IP 10.200.0.1 assigned by networkd\"\n    break\n  fi\n  sleep 1\ndone\n\n# Add WG mesh alias IP — uses existing default gateway\nip addr add \"$ALIAS_IP\" dev \"$IFACE\" 2>/dev/null || echo \"[wg-xray-network] $ALIAS_IP already present\"\n\n# Route to decoy VPS (10.0.0.1 is remote, not on bridge — must go via bridge gateway)\nip route replace 10.0.0.1 via \"$GW\" dev \"$IFACE\"\n\necho \"[wg-xray-network] done\"\n"}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:12:01.712Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"No, it does **not** have to be a WireGuard interface if the decoy is already forwarding plain TCP/UDP traffic to this instance.\n\nWireGuard is only needed if this box is supposed to terminate an encrypted WG tunnel from the decoy/client. If the decoy is doing the tunnel/forwarding and sends traffic onward to Xray, then `10.200.0.1/30` can live on any interface that receives that traffic:\n\n- `eth0` inside `wg-xray`, which is what you already have\n- a dummy interface like `ingress0`\n- a veth/bridge interface\n- a physical-passed Incus NIC\n- `wg0`, only if you specifically want WireGuard termination here\n\nGiven the current state, the simplest model is probably:\n\n```text\ndecoy forwards -> host ovsbr0 10.200.0.2/30 -> wg-xray eth0 10.200.0.1/30 -> xray\n```\n\nThat means no `wg0` is required at all. In fact, forcing `wg0` into this may add failure modes unless WireGuard itself is part of the identity boundary.\n\nCurrent important state I found:\n\n- `wg-xray` already has `10.200.0.1/30` on `eth0`\n- Xray is active and waits for `10.200.0.1` on `eth0`\n- `wgcf-up.service` has been stopped and disabled\n- `wg-quick@wg0.service` is enabled but failing because `/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf` does not exist\n- the old `wg0` backup config uses `Address = 10.0.0.1/24`, not `10.200.0.1/30`\n\nSo if the decoy forwards to this container over the existing host/container link, I would leave `10.200.0.1/30` on `eth0` and disable the broken `wg-quick@wg0.service` to keep boot clean:\n\n```bash\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- systemctl disable --now wg-quick@wg0.service\n```\n\nThe WireGuard layer should only come back if this instance needs to authenticate/decrypt WG peers directly.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}
{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:12:01.717Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"No, it does **not** have to be a WireGuard interface if the decoy is already forwarding plain TCP/UDP traffic to this instance.\n\nWireGuard is only needed if this box is supposed to terminate an encrypted WG tunnel from the decoy/client. If the decoy is doing the tunnel/forwarding and sends traffic onward to Xray, then `10.200.0.1/30` can live on any interface that receives that traffic:\n\n- `eth0` inside `wg-xray`, which is what you already have\n- a dummy interface like `ingress0`\n- a veth/bridge interface\n- a physical-passed Incus NIC\n- `wg0`, only if you specifically want WireGuard termination here\n\nGiven the current state, the simplest model is probably:\n\n```text\ndecoy forwards -> host ovsbr0 10.200.0.2/30 -> wg-xray eth0 10.200.0.1/30 -> xray\n```\n\nThat means no `wg0` is required at all. In fact, forcing `wg0` into this may add failure modes unless WireGuard itself is part of the identity boundary.\n\nCurrent important state I found:\n\n- `wg-xray` already has `10.200.0.1/30` on `eth0`\n- Xray is active and waits for `10.200.0.1` on `eth0`\n- `wgcf-up.service` has been stopped and disabled\n- `wg-quick@wg0.service` is enabled but failing because `/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf` does not exist\n- the old `wg0` backup config uses `Address = 10.0.0.1/24`, not `10.200.0.1/30`\n\nSo if the decoy forwards to this container over the existing host/container link, I would leave `10.200.0.1/30` on `eth0` and disable the broken `wg-quick@wg0.service` to keep boot clean:\n\n```bash\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- systemctl disable --now wg-quick@wg0.service\n```\n\nThe WireGuard layer should only come back if this instance needs to authenticate/decrypt WG peers directly."}],"phase":"final_answer"}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:13:22.883Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Then yes: **WireGuard has to terminate at the place doing identity confirmation**, or that place cannot prove the WG key.\n\nSo the clean model is:\n\n```text\nclient WG key\n  -> decoy forwards UDP/51820\n  -> wg-xray terminates wg0\n  -> identity injector checks wg peer/public key\n  -> Xray receives connection with injected identity\n```\n\nIf the decoy only forwards packets, it does **not** confirm identity. It just passes encrypted WG traffic through.\n\nIf the decoy terminates WireGuard, then `wg-xray` cannot directly confirm the WG key anymore. The decoy would need to forward a signed identity assertion/header to Xray, otherwise the identity is just trust-by-network-path.\n\nSo for your stated requirement, use `wg0` in `wg-xray`.\n\nImportant distinction:\n\n- `wg0` should carry the peer identity/auth boundary.\n- `10.200.0.1/30` does not necessarily need to be on `wg0` unless your Xray/injector expects to bind there.\n- The decoy should forward UDP `51820` to the container’s reachable address.\n- Then systemd should start `wg-quick@wg0.service`, and Xray/injector should start **after** `wg-quick@wg0.service`.\n\nCurrent blocker: `/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf` is missing, and the old backup does not look like the final config. Once your setup generates the real `wg0.conf`, the systemd shape should be:\n\n```bash\nsystemctl enable wg-quick@wg0.service\n```\n\nand Xray should depend on it:\n\n```ini\nAfter=wg-quick@wg0.service\nWants=wg-quick@wg0.service\n```\n\nThen the injector can map identity from:\n\n```bash\nwg show wg0\n```\n\nusing peer public key / allowed IP / latest handshake state.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}
{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:13:22.888Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"Then yes: **WireGuard has to terminate at the place doing identity confirmation**, or that place cannot prove the WG key.\n\nSo the clean model is:\n\n```text\nclient WG key\n  -> decoy forwards UDP/51820\n  -> wg-xray terminates wg0\n  -> identity injector checks wg peer/public key\n  -> Xray receives connection with injected identity\n```\n\nIf the decoy only forwards packets, it does **not** confirm identity. It just passes encrypted WG traffic through.\n\nIf the decoy terminates WireGuard, then `wg-xray` cannot directly confirm the WG key anymore. The decoy would need to forward a signed identity assertion/header to Xray, otherwise the identity is just trust-by-network-path.\n\nSo for your stated requirement, use `wg0` in `wg-xray`.\n\nImportant distinction:\n\n- `wg0` should carry the peer identity/auth boundary.\n- `10.200.0.1/30` does not necessarily need to be on `wg0` unless your Xray/injector expects to bind there.\n- The decoy should forward UDP `51820` to the container’s reachable address.\n- Then systemd should start `wg-quick@wg0.service`, and Xray/injector should start **after** `wg-quick@wg0.service`.\n\nCurrent blocker: `/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf` is missing, and the old backup does not look like the final config. Once your setup generates the real `wg0.conf`, the systemd shape should be:\n\n```bash\nsystemctl enable wg-quick@wg0.service\n```\n\nand Xray should depend on it:\n\n```ini\nAfter=wg-quick@wg0.service\nWants=wg-quick@wg0.service\n```\n\nThen the injector can map identity from:\n\n```bash\nwg show wg0\n```\n\nusing peer public key / allowed IP / latest handshake state."}],"phase":"final_answer"}}

If `10.200.0.1` is the gRPC exposure point for Netmaker, then it should stay on the interface Netmaker can actually route to.\n\nIn the current topology, that sounds like:\n\n```text\nhost / Netmaker side\n  ovsbr0: 10.200.0.2/30\n\nwg-xray instance\n  eth0:   10.200.0.1/30\n```\n\nSo `10.200.0.1/30` belongs on `eth0`, not necessarily `wg0`.\n\nThen `wg0` is only for WireGuard identity proof:\n\n```text\ndecoy forwards UDP/51820 -> wg-xray wg0\nwg-xray confirms peer key -> injector maps identity\ninjector / xray exposes gRPC on 10.200.0.1 via eth0\nNetmaker reaches gRPC through 10.200.0.1\n```\n\nThat separation is cleaner:\n\n- `eth0` / `10.200.0.1/30`: management, gRPC, Netmaker reachability\n- `wg0`: client identity/auth boundary\n- Xray/injector: starts after `wg0` if it needs peer identity, but binds/exposes gRPC on `10.200.0.1`\n\nSo we should **not move `10.200.0.1/30` to `wg0`** if Netmaker depends on reaching it through the current `/30` link. Keep it on `eth0`, and only start/fix `wg0` for identity confirmation.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

Then the correction is:\n\n`10.200.0.1/30` must live on whatever interface actually exists inside the Xray identity-injection namespace.\n\nIf `eth0` is only on the hypervisor side and not inside that namespace, then `eth0` is the wrong place. In that model:\n\n```text\nhypervisor / Netmaker side\n  routes/reaches 10.200.0.1\n\nxray identity namespace\n  wg0 owns 10.200.0.1/30\n  wg0 confirms peer key\n  Xray/gRPC binds on 10.200.0.1\n```\n\nSo yes, for your design, `wg0` is probably the right interface for `10.200.0.1/30` because it is both:\n\n- the WG key confirmation boundary\n- the address Netmaker reaches for gRPC identity injection\n\nOne caveat: when I inspected `wg-xray`, Incus showed an `eth0@if6` inside that container, but that is an Incus veth, not the hypervisor’s physical `eth0`. If your intended identity namespace does not use that veth path, then we should ignore it and make systemd target `wg0`.\n\nThe desired systemd shape is:\n\n```ini\nwg-quick@wg0.service\n  -> adds/loads wg0\n\nwg0-10.200.0.1.service\n  -> ip addr add 10.200.0.1/30 dev wg0\n\nxray.service\n  -> starts after wg0 has 10.200.0.1\n```\n\nAnd Xray should wait on:\n\n```bash\nip -4 addr show dev wg0 | grep -q '10.200.0.1/'\n```\n\nnot `eth0`.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:16:32.690Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, that is the important effect.\n\nIf `wg0` was created on the hypervisor and Incus captures it with:\n\n```bash\nincus config device add wg-xray wg0 nic nictype=physical parent=wg0\n```\n\nthen `wg0` is moved into the `wg-xray` container namespace. From there:\n\n```text\nwg-xray namespace\n  wg0: captured WireGuard ingress / identity key boundary\n  eth0: Incus veth toward host/ovsbr0, if still attached\n```\n\nInside the container, `wg0` and `eth0` can talk to each other through normal Linux routing/firewalling/proxying because they are now in the same network namespace.\n\nSo the capture gives you:\n\n- `wg0` inside the container for WG key confirmation\n- `eth0` inside the container for the `10.200.0.1 <-> 10.200.0.2` gRPC/Netmaker exposure path\n- Xray/injector can see both sides\n\nThat means the clean setup is probably:\n\n```text\ndecoy -> hypervisor external path -> captured wg0 inside wg-xray\nwg-xray confirms WG peer key on wg0\nwg-xray injects identity into Xray\nwg-xray exposes gRPC on 10.200.0.1 over eth0/ovsbr0 to Netmaker\n```\n\nIn that case, keep:\n\n```text\n10.200.0.1/30 on eth0\n```\n\nand use:\n\n```text\nwg0 only for WireGuard ingress / identity\n```\n\nDo **not** alias `10.200.0.1` onto `wg0` unless you want Netmaker/gRPC to ride the WireGuard interface instead of the Incus veth path.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:17:43.015Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, with one naming correction:\n\nIf the Incus device is named `wg0`, the interface **inside the container** can appear as `wg0`, even if the host-side plumbing is Incus/veth/OVS. In that case, putting the alias there is right:\n\n```bash\nip addr add 10.200.0.1/30 dev wg0\nip link set wg0 up\n```\n\nSo the target model becomes:\n\n```text\nhypervisor / Netmaker side\n  10.200.0.2/30\n\nwg-xray container\n  wg0: 10.200.0.1/30\n  xray/gRPC binds or is reached through 10.200.0.1\n```\n\nSystemd should then wait for `wg0`, not `eth0`:\n\n```ini\n[Unit]\nDescription=Add 10.200.0.1/30 to captured wg0\nAfter=network-online.target\nWants=network-online.target\n\n[Service]\nType=oneshot\nRemainAfterExit=yes\nExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'for i in $(seq 1 30); do ip link show wg0 && break; sleep 1; done; ip link set wg0 up; ip addr add 10.200.0.1/30 dev wg0 2>/dev/null || true'\n\n[Install]\nWantedBy=multi-user.target\n```\n\nAnd Xray should check:\n\n```bash\nip -4 addr show dev wg0 | grep -q '10.200.0.1/'\n```\n\nnot `eth0`.\n\nThe only thing I’d be careful about is terminology: if it is true `nictype=physical parent=wg0`, Incus moves the host’s `wg0` into the container. If it is an Incus bridged NIC renamed to `wg0`, then it is veth-backed. Either way, from inside the container the address goes on `wg0`.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}
{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:17:43.026Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"output_text","text":"Yes, with one naming correction:\n\nIf the Incus device is named `wg0`, the interface **inside the container** can appear as `wg0`, even if the host-side plumbing is Incus/veth/OVS. {"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:19:23.367Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"That message usually means something is trying to log in as `root` on the console and PAM rejected the password.\n\nOn a Debian/systemd container or VM, you can inspect it with:\n\n```bash\njournalctl -b | grep -i 'password check for root failed'\njournalctl -b -u console-getty.service\njournalctl -b _COMM=login\n```\n\nIf it is in the `wg-xray` container:\n\n```bash\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- journalctl -b | grep -i 'password check for root failed'\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- journalctl -b -u console-getty.service\n```\n\nCommon causes:\n\n- Someone typed the wrong root password in the noVNC console.\n- An automated console login attempt is configured somewhere.\n- `root` login is disabled or locked, so even the expected password fails.\n- Cloud/container image has no usable root password by default.\n\nCheck root lock status:\n\n```bash\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- passwd -S root\n```\n\nIf you do not need console root password login, this is mostly noise. You can still enter the container safely with:\n\n```bash\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- bash\n```\n\nIf you want root console login to work, set a root password inside the instance:\n\n```bash\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- passwd root\n```","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:21:46.553Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Right. This stack has real ordering dependencies, so trying to “fix” the console/auth symptom before the network graph is stable will be misleading.\n\nThe dependency shape is roughly:\n\n```text\nIncus device capture / interface exists\n  -> wg0 or captured ingress interface has address/routes\n  -> Xray route path is up\n  -> identity injector can map WG peer/key\n  -> gRPC/socket exposure works\n  -> Netmaker can consume/control it\n```\n\nIf Netmaker is moving to sockets, then `10.200.0.1` may become less important for that control path, but Xray still needs its routing and identity boundary correct before the rest is meaningful.\n\nI would defer the noVNC/root-login noise for now unless it blocks access. The actionable network/systemd target is:\n\n- don’t start stale `wgcf`\n- have systemd wait for the captured interface\n- bring up the real WG/ingress path when the correct config exists\n- start Xray only after that route/identity path is ready\n- start Netmaker/socket-facing services after Xray is routable\n\nCurrent useful cleanup already done:\n\n```text\nwgcf-up.service disabled and stopped\nwgcf interface removed from wg-xray\n```\n\nThe broken remaining bit is:\n\n```text\nwg-quick@wg0.service is enabled but failing because /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf is missing\n```\n\nSo once your setup writes the correct `wg0.conf`, that service becomes the next anchor in the boot order.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:24:31.081Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"No, not automatically. Incus only has:\n\n```ini\nRequires=network-online.target lxcfs.service incus.socket\n```\n\nIt does **not** wait for WireGuard unless we explicitly add that ordering.\n\nAlso, right now on the host:\n\n- no `wg0` interface is up\n- there is no `/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf`\n- host WireGuard configs are named things like `netmaker.conf`, `opdbus.conf`, `wg-decoy.conf`, `chatbot.conf`\n- `wg-xray` does not currently have a physical captured `wg0` device attached\n\nSo if the correct host config is, for example, `/etc/wireguard/wg-decoy.conf`, then `wg-quick@wg-decoy.service` would create interface `wg-decoy`, not `wg0`.\n\nYour idea is right though: if the host brings up the correct WG interface first, then Incus captures it with `nictype=physical`, the container does **not** need to run WireGuard. It just receives an already-configured interface.\n\nThe boot order needs to be made explicit:\n\n```ini\n# incus.service override\n[Unit]\nAfter=wg-quick@wg0.service\nRequires=wg-quick@wg0.service\n```\n\nBut only if the config file is actually `/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf`.\n\nIf the real config is `/etc/wireguard/wg-decoy.conf`, then either capture `parent=wg-decoy`, or rename/copy it to `wg0.conf` so the interface name is `wg0`.\n\nClean target:\n\n```text\nhost systemd starts WireGuard interface\nIncus starts after that\nIncus physical-captures WG interface into wg-xray\ncontainer does not run wg-quick\ncontainer only aliases/routes/binds services on captured interface\n```","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:25:12.509Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Yes, I think that’s the right simplification.\n\nIf the decoy is now the trust/isolation boundary, then the container does **not** need clever NIC capture just to protect the host. Let Incus/OVS provide a normal managed link, and keep identity/routing logic at the service layer.\n\nSimpler model:\n\n```text\ndecoy\n  forwards ingress traffic\n\nhost\n  Netmaker / management\n  ovsbr0: 10.200.0.2/30\n\nwg-xray container\n  eth0 on Incus-managed ovsbr0\n  10.200.0.1/30\n  Xray / identity injector\n```\n\nThen avoid:\n\n- `nictype=physical parent=wg0`\n- moving WG interfaces between namespaces\n- running WireGuard in both host and container\n- depending on Incus boot ordering around WG capture\n\nKeep:\n\n```text\n10.200.0.1/30 on container eth0\n10.200.0.2/30 on host ovsbr0\nXray binds/exposes on 10.200.0.1\ndecoy forwards to that path\n```\n\nGiven what we saw, your current setup is already close to this:\n\n- `wg-xray` has `eth0` inside the container\n- `eth0` already has `10.200.0.1/30`\n- host `ovsbr0` already has `10.200.0.2/30`\n- Xray is already running\n- `wgcf-up.service` is disabled now\n- the broken thing is `wg-quick@wg0.service`, which should probably be disabled if you abandon WG capture\n\nThat cleanup command would be:\n\n```bash\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- systemctl disable --now wg-quick@wg0.service\n```\n\nThen treat WireGuard/Netmaker as host/decoy infrastructure, and let the container just be the Xray identity-injection service endpoint on OVS.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T06:29:58.795Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"Correct. `wgcf register` creates the account file:\n\n```text\n/root/wgcf-account.toml\n```\n\nThen `wgcf generate` uses that account file to create the WireGuard profile:\n\n```text\nwgcf-profile.conf\n```\n\nSo after reboot, the clean interactive sequence is:\n\n```bash\nsudo incus exec wg-xray -- bash\ncd /root\nwgcf register\nwgcf generate --profile /etc/wireguard/wgcf-profile.conf\ncp -a /etc/wireguard/wgcf-profile.conf /etc/wireguard/wgcf.conf\nchmod 600 /root/wgcf-account.toml /etc/wireguard/wgcf-profile.conf /etc/wireguard/wgcf.conf\n```\n\nAnd because `wgcf-up.service` is disabled, generating the config will not automatically start it.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}
