I'll have a detailed breakdown ready once it completes — including the WireGuard session derivation, NextDNS header injection, gRPC forwarding logic, and how that maps to the concert/wristband/valet analogy.\n\nHere's the full breakdown of the zero-trust identity pipeline, mapped to the concert analogy throughout.\n\nThe Concert Analogy\nYou arrive at a venue. You hand your keys to the valet (WireGuard). The valet parks your car and gives you a claim ticket (session ID). At the door, you exchange the ticket for an all-access wristband (the Ghostbridge identity sled). Every backstage door checks the wristband — not your car, not your ticket — just the wristband. Your car (the WireGuard tunnel) never enters the venue.\n\nStage 1 — The Valet: WireGuard Handshake & Session ID Derivation\nFiles: crates/op-gateway/src/wireguard_auth.rs:529-633\n\nWhen a peer connects over WireGuard, the gateway derives three cryptographic artifacts:\n\nSession ID (the claim ticket)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:529-540\nlet input = format!(\"WG-SESSION-{}-{}\", peer_pubkey, Self::current_timestamp());\nlet session_ids = self.crypto_engine.generate_session_ids_batch(&[input.as_bytes()]);\n// → BLAKE2s hash → 128-bit hex string\nInput: Curve25519 peer public key + current timestamp\nAlgorithm: SIMD-accelerated BLAKE2s\nOutput: 16-byte hex session ID — the peer's claim ticket\nPSK (stable parking spot number)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:542-593\nlet salt = b\"WG-STABLE-PSK-2024\";  // fixed — no timestamp\n// Argon2 KDF over peer pubkey\nDeliberately does not rotate — rotating it would lock peers out mid-session, like changing the valet lot number while cars are still parked.\n\nSession Key (per-visit ephemeral)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:595-633\nlet server_nonce = self.generate_server_nonce().await?;\n// Argon2 + nonce → ephemeral key, rotated per connection\nThe Session Record (the claim stub kept by the valet)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:200-215\npub struct WireGuardSession {\n    pub session_id: String,        // BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp)\n    pub peer_pubkey: String,\n    pub psk: String,               // stable Argon2\n    pub expires_at: u64,           // 1 hour TTL\n    pub auth_method: String,       // \"wireguard\"\n    pub key_rotation_count: u32,\n    // ...\n}\nPersisted to SQLite (wireguard_sessions table) and cached in DashMap (no SQL in the hot path).\n\nStage 2 — The Wristband Printer: IdentitySled\nFiles: crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/sled.rs, crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs\n\nOnce the WireGuard session is established, a 152-byte shared-memory struct (/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat) is stamped — the all-access wristband:\n\nIdentitySled layout (repr(C), 152 bytes):\n  [ 0.. 32]  wireguard_pubkey    — who you are\n  [32.. 40]  mutation_index      — which version of the schema you authenticated against\n  [40.. 72]  hashed_footprint    — Blake3(current schema state) — the hologram on the wristband\n  [72.. 88]  trace_id            — UUID v4 — your unique wristband serial number\n  [88.. 92]  schema_version\n  [92..152]  reserved\n  [192..208] nextdns_profile     — e.g., \"689ec7\" — your VIP section access\nThe footprint (Blake3 hash of the live schema state) is the hologram — it proves the wristband was issued by tonight's venue, not a forgery from last week's show.\n\nThe trace_id is the serial number stamped on your wrist — immutable, linked to a Qdrant vector record for full accountability.\n\nNextDNS Profile (the VIP section pass)\n# deploy/nextdns/upsert-rewrite.py\n# Profile ID: 689ec7\n# Upserts DNS rewrites: dashboard.3tched.com → 10.0.0.1\nThe NextDNS profile ID travels with the identity sled. It tells the DNS layer which routing rules apply to this peer — their section of the venue.\n\nStage 3 — The Door Scanner: xray Header Injection\nFile: deploy/incus/privacy-xray-ingress/etc/xray/config.json:47-50\n\nxray sits at the venue entrance. It reads the wristband (sled) and stamps the metadata onto every gRPC call:\n\n\"grpcSettings\": {\n  \"serviceName\": \"Ghostbridge.StateSync\",\n  \"multiMode\": true,\n  \"metadata\": {\n    \"X-Ghostbridge-Footprint\": \"<Blake3 footprint hex>\",\n    \"X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID\":  \"<UUID v4 hex>\"\n  }\n}\nAt this point, WireGuard is dropped. The tunnel delivered the peer to the door; the tunnel itself does not go backstage. xray strips the WireGuard framing and forwards a plain gRPC call carrying only the two header stamps. The car stays in the lot.\n\nThe NextDNS profile influences DNS resolution at this layer — selector_ip routing directs packets to the correct Incus container before they ever reach the gRPC endpoint.\n\nStage 4 — The Backstage Guard: GhostbridgeInterceptor\nFile: crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/interceptor.rs:34-84\n\nEvery gRPC call hits this Tonic middleware on port 18789 before any handler sees it:\n\npub fn ghostbridge_interceptor(mut req: Request<()>) -> Result<Request<()>, Status> {\n    // 1. Wristband must be present\n    let footprint_value = req.metadata().get(\"x-ghostbridge-footprint\").cloned();\n    let trace_value    = req.metadata().get(\"x-ghostbridge-trace-id\").cloned();\n\n    if footprint_value.is_none() || trace_value.is_none() {\n        return Err(Status::unauthenticated(\n            \"A.N.N.A. Scribe: Missing Ghostbridge Identity Sled. Connection Dropped.\",\n        ));\n    }\n\n    // 2. Zero-copy mmap read of the live sled (no DB hit, no network hop)\n    let (sled_ptr, _mmap) = op_identity::read_sled()?;\n    let sled = unsafe { &*sled_ptr };\n\n    // 3. Hologram check — footprint must match tonight's schema state exactly\n    let expected_footprint = hex::encode(sled.hashed_footprint);\n    if request_footprint != expected_footprint {\n        return Err(Status::permission_denied(\n            \"A.N.N.A. Scribe: Temporal Hash Mismatch. Session footprint out of sync.\",\n        ));\n    }\n\n    // 4. Embed trace ID into gRPC extensions for downstream accountability\n    req.extensions_mut().insert(trace_val);\n    Ok(req)\n}\nValidity rule: the sled is live only if hashed_footprint != [0u8;32] AND trace_id != [0u8;16]. A zero field means the wristband was never properly stamped — instant ejection.\n\nThe check is zero-copy — the sled lives in tmpfs (/dev/shm), mmap'd directly into the process. No SQL, no network, no disk. The guard glances at your wrist under UV light in milliseconds.\n\nStage 5 — Backstage: gRPC Routing to op-dbus\nFile: crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/main.rs:94-105\n\nOnce the interceptor passes the call, it routes to the internal gRPC service:\n\nDefault: http://10.200.0.2:50051  (op-dbus, inside the privacy network)\nSubnet assignments per peer come from schemas/plugin/privacy_routes.json:\n\n{\n  \"wireguard_public_key\": \"P8c9Kjnv4B3r6C4+...\",\n  \"assigned_ip\":  \"10.100.0.2/32\",    // WireGuard tunnel allocation\n  \"selector_ip\":  \"10.100.0.2\",       // OpenFlow packet-match label\n  \"container_name\": \"privacy-route-550e8400\"\n}\nOpenFlow matches selector_ip and routes to the correct Incus container. The WireGuard subnet (10.100.0.0/24) exists only to give each peer a unique identity label — it is never forwarded as a WireGuard packet beyond the gateway.\n\nA Linux user session (wg-{first12ofpubkey}) is created via loginctl enable-linger, giving the peer a D-Bus session and $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR — the backstage room with their name on the door.\n\nComplete Flow, Annotated\n[Peer]\n  │  WireGuard UDP (Curve25519 handshake)\n  ▼\n[op-gateway / WireGuard endpoint]\n  │  BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp) → session_id        ← claim ticket issued\n  │  Argon2(pubkey, stable-salt) → PSK               ← stable parking spot\n  │  Argon2(pubkey, nonce)       → session_key        ← tonight's coat check\n  │  Write IdentitySled → /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat  ← wristband stamped\n  │\n  │  WireGuard framing DROPPED here ──────────────────← car stays with valet\n  ▼\n[xray ingress]\n  │  Reads sled: footprint + trace_id + nextdns_profile\n  │  Injects gRPC metadata headers:\n  │    X-Ghostbridge-Footprint: <blake3-hex>\n  │    X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID:  <uuid4-hex>\n  │  NextDNS profile → DNS rewrites applied (VIP section routing)\n  ▼\n[GhostbridgeInterceptor — port 18789]\n  │  Header present? No  → 403 \"Temporal Hash Mismatch\"\n  │  Zero-copy mmap sled read (tmpfs, no DB)\n  │  Inject trace_id into gRPC extensions\n  ▼\n[op-dbus gRPC — 10.200.0.2:50051]\n  │  Full access to internal services\n  │  Trace ID rides every call → Qdrant vector linkage for audit\n  ▼\n[Incus container — privacy-route-{user_id}]\n  └─ Linux user session, D-Bus activated, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR alive\nWhy This Is Genuinely Zero-Trust\nZero-Trust Principle\tImplementation\nNever trust, always verify\tEvery gRPC call re-validates the live sled footprint — no cached \"logged in\" state\nVerify cryptographic state, not identity claims\tFootprint is Blake3 of current schema — a stale wristband from an old schema is invalid\nLeast privilege\tNextDNS profile scopes DNS; assigned_ip/32 scopes the subnet to exactly one peer\nFull audit trail\tTrace ID links every call to a Qdrant vector record — immutable, append-only\nNo implicit trust from network location\tBeing inside 10.100.0.0/24 grants nothing — the wristband check happens regardless\nThe WireGuard subnet is purely a cryptographic identity label — it gets the peer through the front door and into the valet system. {"timestamp":"2026-06-08T11:51:08.332Z","type":"event_msg","payload":{"type":"agent_message","message":"You’re right: the recent WireGuard handshake is not the thing cognitive-mcp should trust. The issue is the wristband handoff.\n\nWhat I found:\n\n- `op-cognitive-mcp` only writes the sled if `WG_PUBKEY` is preassigned. It does **not** derive the local identity from `wg show` in this path: [wireguard.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-identity/src/wireguard.rs:25).\n- The installed service does not set `WG_PUBKEY`; it only sets empty `WG_INTERFACE`: [/etc/s6/sv/op-cognitive-mcp/run](/etc/s6/sv/op-cognitive-mcp/run:4).\n- cognitive-mcp then logs exactly that failure path: “`WG_PUBKEY not set ... identity sled not written`”.\n- The live sled path expected by the Shuttle/interceptor is `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat`: [schema_bridge.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs:270).\n- `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` is currently missing.\n- There is a valid-looking stale/disk sled at `/var/lib/op-dbus/plugin_schema.dat`, but its pubkey is `iNqgBk7pBC/iXUmF+v4PNvvdAxjP5qWjxzMYYRE8+hw=`, not the `op_dbus` key you showed: `BhFpzRSQTPXxRhNBXbQUXhOQz4nxeV3EJ4d3JH07c2U=`.\n\nSo the root cause is not “no WireGuard handshake.” It’s that the detached identity was never injected into the cognitive-mcp process as `WG_PUBKEY`, and the live wristband file in tmpfs was never stamped. The handshake exists at the valet, but the wristband printer has no assigned identity input.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

It does **not** derive the local identity from `wg show` in this path: [wireguard.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-identity/src/wireguard.rs:25).\n- The installed service does not set `WG_PUBKEY`; it only sets empty `WG_INTERFACE`: [/etc/s6/sv/op-cognitive-mcp/run](/etc/s6/sv/op-cognitive-mcp/run:4).\n- cognitive-mcp then logs exactly that failure path: “`WG_PUBKEY not set ... identity sled not written`”.\n- The live sled path expected by the Shuttle/interceptor is `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat`: [schema_bridge.rs](/home/jeremy/git/operation-dbus-proto/crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs:270).\n- `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` is currently missing.\n- There is a valid-looking stale/disk sled at `/var/lib/op-dbus/plugin_schema.dat`, but its pubkey is `iNqgBk7pBC/iXUmF+v4PNvvdAxjP5qWjxzMYYRE8+hw=`, not the `op_dbus` key you showed: `BhFpzRSQTPXxRhNBXbQUXhOQz4nxeV3EJ4d3JH07c2U=`.\n\nSo the root cause is not “no WireGuard handshake.” It’s that the detached identity was never injected into the cognitive-mcp process as `WG_PUBKEY`, and the live wristband file in tmpfs was never stamped. The handshake exists at the valet, but the wristband printer has no assigned identity input.","completed_at":1780919468,"duration_ms":37776,"time_to_first_token_ms":11788}}

It’s printing either a random UUID, a synthetic pubkey/mutation string, or nothing.\n\nThe correct fix is to thread the gateway `session_id` into sled stamping as the canonical `trace_id`/Snowball session field, then have xray and gRPC metadata inject exactly that sled value. The current injection path is disconnected from the WireGuard session derivation.","phase":"final_answer","memory_citation":null}}

CozoDB References & Connection Configuration\\n\\n**Core implementation**: `crates/op-cozo-store/src/lib.rs` (single file crate)\\n- `CozoGraphShuttle` struct wraps `Arc<DbInstance>` (Sled storage engine)\\n- `new_persistent(path)` — opens sled-backed CozoDB at given path\\n- `new_in_memory()` — ephemeral for tests\\n- `from_env()` — reads `COGNITIVE_MCP_COZO_DB_PATH` or falls back to in-memory\\n\\n**Schema relations seeded on startup** (from `seed_schema`):\\n- `compliance_rule`, `subid_registry`, `graph_node`, `graph_edge`, `audit_event`\\n- `users`, `sessions`\\n- `memory_namespaces`, `memory_entries` — the actual memory store\\n\\n**Consumers**:\\n\\n| Consumer | File | How it gets CozoDB |\\n|----------|------|--------------------|\\n| `CognitiveMcpServer` | `server.rs:41` | `CozoGraphShuttle::new_persistent(db_path)` via CLI `--db` |\\n| `CognitiveMemoryStore` | `memory_store.rs:115` | Takes `Arc<CozoGraphShuttle>` — wraps CozoDB with typed namespace CRUD |\\n| `op-cog-admin` CLI | `op-cog-admin.rs:35` | `CozoGraphShuttle::new_persistent(cli.db)` |\\n| `op-chat` | `op-chat/src/main.rs:32` | `CozoGraphShuttle::new_persistent(db_path)` from `OP_MEMORY_DB` env |\\n| `op-assistant-grpc` | `op-assistant-grpc/src/server.rs:78-80` | In-memory or persistent from `cfg.cozo_db_path` |\\n\\n**Environment variables for CozoDB path**:\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_DB_PATH` — used by main binary and s6 run script\\n- `OP_MEMORY_DB` — used by op-chat and op-web-srv (s6)\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_COZO_DB_PATH` — used by `CozoGraphShuttle::from_env()`\\n- `OP_ASSISTANT_COZO_PATH` — spec'd for op-assistant-grpc\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 4. QdrantSemanticShuttle Analysis (`qdrant_shuttle.rs` — 725 lines)\\n\\n**Architecture**: Clean, well-structured shuttle with two distinct responsibilities:\\n\\n1. **Accountability Trace** (Schema-driven):\\n   - Reads `IdentitySled` from `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` via mmap\\n   - Reads live schema from `/dev/shm/live-schema.json`\\n   - Generates trace IDs from hashed footprint: `trace-{hex(hashed_footprint)}`\\n   - Queries Qdrant `ctl_plane_reasoning_episodes` collection filtered by trace_id\\n   - Embeds schema text via Voyage AI for semantic search within trace\\n\\n2. **User Memory** (Namespace-scoped):\\n   - `upsert_user_memory()` — stores point with `container_id`, `entry_key`, `content` payload\\n   - `search_user_memory()` — semantic search filtered by `container_id`\\n   - Uses Voyage AI embeddings (1024-dim, `voyage-4` model)\\n\\n**Configuration (all via env vars)**:\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_QDRANT_URL` → default `http://127.0.0.1:6334`\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_QDRANT_COLLECTION` → default `ctl_plane_reasoning_episodes`\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_USER_MEMORY_COLLECTION` → default `user_memory`\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_SCHEMA_SLED_PATH` → default `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat`\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_KEY` / `VOYAGE_API_KEY` → required\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_URL` → default Voyage public endpoint\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_QUERY_MODEL` → default `voyage-4`\\n- `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_OUTPUT_DIMENSION` → default `1024`\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 5. VoyageClient Implementations — THREE Separate Copies!\\n\\n| Location | Struct | Fields | Env Vars | Default Model |\\n|----------|--------|--------|----------|---------------|\\n| `voyage.rs:12` | `pub VoyageClient` | `client, api_key, model, base_url` | `VOYAGE_API_KEY`, `VOYAGE_MODEL` | `voyage-4` |\\n| `qdrant_shuttle.rs:319` | `struct VoyageClient` (private) | `client, api_url, api_key, model, output_dimension` | `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_KEY`/`VOYAGE_API_KEY`, `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_URL`, `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_QUERY_MODEL`, `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_OUTPUT_DIMENSION` | `voyage-4` |\\n| `rag_pipeline.rs:184` | `RagPipeline` (inline, not a VoyageClient struct) | `voyage_key, voyage_model, http` | `VOYAGE_API_KEY`/`COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_API_KEY`, `COGNITIVE_MCP_VOYAGE_MODEL`/`VOYAGE_MODEL` | `voyage-4` |\\n\\n**Key differences**:\\n- `voyage.rs` has auto-detect for MongoDB-hosted keys (`al-*` prefix → `ai.mongodb.com`)\\n- `qdrant_shuttle.rs` has `output_dimension` (1024) and separate `input_type` for query vs document\\n- `rag_pipeline.rs` also has MongoDB URL detection logic but inline\\n\\n**⚠️ This is triple-redundant code that needs consolidation.**\\n\\n---\\n\\n### 6. :\\n\\njeremy hobson\\nHow do I use Gemini Code Assist?what is my tier and ratelimit in this session\\n\\n\\nGemini\\nResponding with gemini-3-pro\\nThinking\\nGemini Code Assist is an AI-powered coding companion designed to help you write, debug, and understand code faster. Here is how you can use it effectively, followed by information regarding your account details.\\n\\nHow to use Gemini Code Assist\\nYou can interact with Gemini Code Assist in several ways within your IDE (such as VS Code, IntelliJ, or Cloud Workstations) or the Google Cloud Console.\\n\\nGenerate Code: You can ask Gemini to write functions, classes, or entire scripts. Be specific about the language and the logic you need.\\n\\nExample: \\\"Write a Python function to parse a CSV file and calculate the average of the 'price' column.\\\"\\nExplain Code: If you are looking at a complex piece of legacy code, highlight it and ask Gemini to explain what it does.\\n\\nExample: \\\"Explain the selected code block and identify any potential edge cases.\\\"\\nDebug and Fix Errors: Paste an error message or highlight a buggy function and ask for a fix.\\n\\nExample: \\\"I'm getting a NullPointerException in this method. How do I fix it?\\\"\\nRefactor and Optimize: Ask for suggestions to make your code cleaner or more efficient.\\n\\nExample: \\\"Refactor this Java method to use streams instead of a for-loop.\\\"\\nUnit Tests: Ask Gemini to generate test cases for your existing code.\\n\\nExample: \\\"Generate JUnit tests for this class, covering both success and failure scenarios.\\\"\\nYour Tier and Rate Limit\\nAs an AI assistant, I do not have access to your personal account details, subscription tier, or real-time rate limits for this specific session. I cannot see your billing information or current quota usage.\\n\\nTo find this information, you should check the following resources:\\n\\nGoogle Cloud Console: Navigate to the Billing or Quotas section to see your project's specific limits and usage.\\nIDE Status Bar: In some IDE extensions, clicking the Gemini status icon may reveal connection status or account type.\\nAdministrator: If you are using an enterprise license, your organization's Google Cloud administrator can provide details on the specific tier and quotas assigned to your user or project.\\nGenerated by Gemini 3 Pro Preview\\n\\njeremy hobson\\nwhere are the authentication file stored for code aasit vscode extension\\n\\n\\nGemini\\nResponding with gemini-3-pro\\nThinking\\nGemini Code Assist in VS Code is powered by the Google Cloud Code extension. The location of your authentication credentials depends on how you signed in (via the IDE's built-in OAuth flow or via the gcloud CLI) and your operating system.\\n\\nHere is the breakdown of where these files and states are typically stored.\\n\\n1. VS Code Secret Storage (Primary Method)\\nModern versions of the Cloud Code extension utilize the VS Code Secret Storage API. This means your actual access tokens and refresh tokens are not stored in a plain text file. Instead, they are encrypted and stored in your operating system's native keychain:\\n\\nWindows: Windows Credential Manager\\nmacOS: macOS Keychain\\nLinux: GNOME Keyring or KWallet (via libsecret)\\n2. Extension Global Storage (Metadata & Cache)\\nWhile the secrets are in the keychain, the extension stores authentication metadata, session configuration, and cached states in VS Code's globalStorage directory. If you are trying to clear a corrupted session, this is often the folder you need to check.\\n\\nWindows:\\n\\ntext\\n%APPDATA%\\\\Code\\\\User\\\\globalStorage\\\\googlecloudtools.cloudcode\\nmacOS:\\n\\ntext\\n~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/globalStorage/googlecloudtools.cloudcode\\nLinux:\\n\\ntext\\n~/.config/Code/User/globalStorage/googlecloudtools.cloudcode\\n3. Google Cloud CLI (gcloud) Storage\\nIf you authenticated using the Google Cloud CLI (e.g., running gcloud auth login) and the extension is utilizing that credential set, the files are stored in the standard gcloud configuration directory.\\n\\nWindows:\\n\\ntext\\n%APPDATA%\\\\gcloud\\nmacOS / Linux:\\n\\ntext\\n~/.config/gcloud\\nTroubleshooting Tip\\nIf you are asking this because you are stuck in an authentication loop or facing login issues, deleting the specific \\\"file\\\" might not be enough due to the OS keychain integration.\\n\\nThe cleanest way to reset your authentication state is usually:\\n\\nSign out via the Cloud Code status bar in VS Code.\\nRun the \\\"Cloud Code: Sign Out\\\" command from the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P).\\nIf issues persist, you may need to manually remove the googlecloudtools.cloudcode entry from your OS Keychain/Credential Manager.\\nGenerated by Gemini 3 Pro Preview\\n\\njeremy hobson\\nwhat scopes does vscode code assist extension use\\n\\n\\nGemini\\nResponding with gemini-3-pro\\nThinking\\nThe Gemini Code Assist features in VS Code are delivered through the Google Cloud Code extension. To function correctly—allowing you to not only chat with the AI but also deploy applications, view logs, and manage resources—the extension requests a specific set of OAuth 2.0 scopes during the login process.\\n\\nHere are the primary scopes used:\\n\\n1. The \\\"Cloud Platform\\\" Scope\\nScope URL: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform\\n\\nThis is the most critical scope. It grants the extension full access to view and manage your data across Google Cloud Platform services.\\n\\nWhy it is needed: Gemini Code Assist needs this to interact with the Gemini for Google Cloud API (specifically the cloudaicompanion.googleapis.com service).\\nBroader Context: Since the extension is also a general-purpose DevOps tool, this scope allows it to deploy to Cloud Run, manage GKE clusters, read Cloud Storage buckets, and view Cloud Logging entries without needing you to re-authenticate for every single service.\\n2. User Identity Scopes\\nScope URLs:\\n\\nemail\\nprofile\\nopenid\\nThese are standard OpenID Connect scopes.\\n\\nWhy they are needed: They allow the extension to identify who you are. This is crucial for billing and quota attribution (checking if your user account has a valid Gemini Code Assist license) and for audit logging.\\nImportant Security Note regarding IAM\\nWhile the cloud-platform scope is broad, it does not grant the extension more power than your user account actually possesses.\\n\\nThe extension acts on your behalf. If your user account (IAM principal) only has the Cloud AI Companion User role and no other permissions, the extension will only be able to use the AI features. It will fail if it tries to delete a virtual machine or drop a database, even though the scope requested was broad, because the underlying IAM permission is missing.\\n\\nGenerated by Gemini 3 Pro Preview\\n\\njeremy hobson\\nwhat apis and services does vscode code assist use\\n\\n\\nGemini\\nResponding with gemini-3-pro\\nSummarizing the APIs\\nGemini Code Assist in VS Code (part of the Google Cloud Code extension) relies on a specific set of Google Cloud APIs to function. If you are configuring a firewall or auditing network traffic, these are the specific endpoints and services you need to be aware of.\\n\\n1. Core AI Service\\nThis is the primary API that powers the \\\"intelligence\\\" of the extension (chat, code generation, and completion).\\n\\nAPI Endpoint: cloudaicompanion.googleapis.com\\nService Name: Gemini for Google Cloud API (formerly Cloud AI Companion API)\\nPurpose: Handles all prompts sent to the LLM, context processing, and returns the generated code or chat responses.\\n2. Authentication & Configuration\\nThese services handle your login state and ensure your Google Cloud project is correctly configured to pay for and authorize the AI usage.\\n\\noauth2.googleapis.com: Used to perform the initial OAuth 2.0 handshake to sign you in.\\nserviceusage.googleapis.com: Used by the extension to verify that the Gemini for Google Cloud API is actually enabled in your selected project.\\ncloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com: Used to list and select the Google Cloud projects you have access to.\\npeople.googleapis.com: Used to fetch your user profile information (like your avatar) for the UI.\\n3. Internal & Telemetry Services\\nThese are internal Google APIs used for IDE-specific functionality and product improvement.\\n\\ncloudcode-pa.googleapis.com: An internal API that provides specific backend features for the Cloud Code extension.\\nfirebaselogging-pa.googleapis.com: Used to send telemetry data, such as whether you accepted or rejected a code suggestion (used to calculate acceptance rates and improve the model).\\nfeedback-pa.googleapis.com: Handles data submission if you use the \\\"Send Feedback\\\" form within the IDE.\\nSummary for Firewall Rules\\nIf you are behind a strict corporate firewall, you generally need to allow outbound TCP traffic (port 443) to these domains. This is a common workflow in enterprise environments where the default Google Cloud Code client ID is restricted by organization policies.\\n\\nTo access your Enterprise benefits (like the full Gemini Code Assist features), you must complete two distinct steps:\\n\\nAuthenticate using your custom OAuth client.\\nSelect the Google Cloud Project that holds your Gemini Code Assist license.\\nHere is how to set this up.\\n\\nStep 1: Create your OAuth Client (Prerequisite)\\nIf you haven't already, you need to create a \\\"Desktop App\\\" OAuth client in the Google Cloud Console.\\n\\nGo to APIs & Services > Credentials.\\nClick Create Credentials > OAuth client ID.\\nApplication type: Desktop app.\\nCopy the Client ID and Client Secret.\\nStep 2: Authenticate via gcloud with Custom Credentials\\nYou can force the gcloud CLI to use your specific client ID and secret instead of the default Google ones. State Desynchronization and Nonce Reuse in ChaCha20-Poly1305 (Critical)\n    16\t* **Impact**: Total loss of confidentiality and integrity of stored WireGuard keys.\n    17\t* **Mechanism**: \n    18\t  In `crates/op-gateway/src/encrypted_storage.rs`, the `MasterKey` struct initializes its stateful `nonce_counter` to `0` when loaded from disk:\n    19\t  ```rust\n    20\t  // Line 307\n    21\t  self.master_key = Some(MasterKey {\n    22\t      key,\n    23\t      salt,\n    24\t      nonce_counter: 0,\n    25\t  });\n    26\t  ```\n    27\t  During the `store_key` flow (line 368), the stateful counter is used to construct the nonce:\n    28\t  ```rust\n    29\t  let nonce_counter = master_key.nonce_counter;\n    30\t  nonce[4..12].copy_from_slice(&nonce_counter.to_le_bytes());\n    31\t  master_key.nonce_counter += 1;\n    32\t  ```\n    33\t  Every time the gateway daemon restarts, the `nonce_counter` resets to `0`. Consequently, writing new keys after a restart reuses previous nonces under the identical master key. In ChaCha20-Poly1305, encrypting two different messages with the same key and nonce allows an attacker to XOR the ciphertexts together to recover the plaintexts and forge valid authentication tags.\n    34\t* **Remediation**:\n    35\t  Switch to generating standard 96-bit random nonces for every encryption operation:\n    36\t  ```rust\n    37\t  let mut nonce = [0u8; 12];\n    38\t  SystemRandom::new().fill(&mut nonce)\n    39\t      .map_err(|_| anyhow::anyhow!(\"Entropy failure\"))?;\n    40\t  ```\n    41\t\n    42\t---\n    43\t\n    44\t#### 2. Predictable Session ID / Auth Token Generation (Critical)\n    45\t* **Impact**: Authentication bypass. Any network attacker can hijack active authenticated sessions.\n    46\t* **Mechanism**: \n    47\t  The `session_id` acts as the primary authentication token when routing client requests through the MCP Gateway. However, `generate_session_id` constructs the token deterministically using public values:\n    48\t  ```rust\n    49\t  // Line 442\n    50\t  let input = format!(\"WG-SESSION-{}-{}\", peer_pubkey, Self::current_timestamp());\n    51\t  let session_ids = self\n    52\t      .crypto_engine\n    53\t      .generate_session_ids_batch(&[input.as_bytes()]);\n    54\t  ```\n    55\t  Because `peer_pubkey` is public and `current_timestamp()` is evaluated in seconds, there are only 3,600 possible session ID combinations per hour for any given peer. An attacker can precalculate these IDs and query the D-Bus or gRPC interface to hijack active client sessions.\n    56\t* **Remediation**:\n    57\t  Inject cryptographically secure random entropy into the session token:\n    58\t  ```rust\n    59\t  let mut token = [0u8; 32];\n    60\t  SystemRandom::new().fill(&mut token)\n    61\t      .map_err(|_| anyhow::anyhow!(\"Entropy failure\"))?;\n    62\t  let session_id = hex::encode(token);\n    63\t  ```\n    64\t\n    65\t---\n    66\t\n    67\t#### 3. Zero-Security WireGuard PSK Derived from Public Metadata (Critical)\n    68\t* **Impact**: Total compromise of WireGuard transport security. Any passive eavesdropper can decrypt VPN payloads.\n    69\t* **Mechanism**: \n    70\t  The preshared key (PSK) used for WireGuard connections is derived using the client's public key as the sole high-entropy input:\n    71\t  ```rust\n    72\t  // Line 545\n    73\t  let salt = b\"WG-STABLE-PSK-2024\";\n    74\t  let mut input = Vec::with_capacity(39);\n    75\t  input.extend_from_slice(b\"WG-PSK-\");\n    76\t  input.extend_from_slice(peer_key);\n    77\t  ```\n    78\t  Because the peer public key is public (by design and transmitted in cleartext during handshakes), the \"preshared key\" is not actually a secret. It can be derived by any entity observing the connection.\n    79\t* **Remediation**:\n    80\t  Use standard cryptographic random values for PSKs and store them within a secure database table accessible only by the gateway process.\n    81\t\n    82\t---\n    83\t\n    84\t#### 4. Master Key Plaintext Exposure in Unencrypted Fallback Directory (High)\n    85\t* **Impact**: Local privilege escalation. Any local process with read access to the directory can read the master key.\n    86\t* **Mechanism**: \n    87\t  In `encrypted_storage.rs:156`, if native experimental Btrfs encryption is not supported, the code falls back silently to an unencrypted subvolume or standard directory:\n    88\t  ```rust\n    89\t  warn!(\"Native Btrfs encryption not supported, creating regular subvolume\");\n    90\t  self.create_regular_subvolume().await?;\n"}}

D-Bus Registration & Policy Analysis\n     4\t* **D-Bus Interfaces, Methods, and Signals**: No D-Bus interfaces, methods, or signals are registered in the audited files (`op-mcp-proxy`). Although other workspace crates depend on `zbus`, this specific crate (`op-mcp-proxy`) acts as a network-to-gRPC proxy and does not register with any D-Bus system or session bus.\n     5\t* **Caller Identity & Verification**: Not applicable for D-Bus. IPC/Network State Mutation & Process Spawning\n    10\tThe following methods and entry points trigger external process execution or invoke billing-heavy external state modifications without authorization:\n    11\t* **WireGuard Process Spawning**:\n    12\t  * `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/session.rs:100` spawns `wg show wg0 public-key` to identify the host machine.\n    13\t  * `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/session.rs:118` spawns `wg show wg0 allowed-ips` to parse peer IP associations.\n    14\t* **Google Cloud CLI Process Spawning**:\n    15\t  * `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/gcloud_auth.rs:230` and `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/gcloud_auth.rs:247` spawn `gcloud auth print-access-token` and `gcloud auth application-default print-access-token` respectively.\n    16\t* **Unauthenticated HTTP State Mutation**:\n    17\t  * `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/http_server.rs:141` (`chat_completions`) exposes LLM endpoints to arbitrary callers over the network without API key validation or authentication. These endpoints invoke costly Vertex AI or CloudAI APIs.\n    18\t\n    19\t### 3. Unvalidated Deserialization\n    20\tThe following endpoints parse caller-supplied bytes without prior validation:\n    21\t* **JSON-RPC Deserialization**:\n    22\t  * `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/main.rs:113` parses standard input directly into a mutable `simd_json::OwnedValue` using `unsafe { simd_json::from_str(&mut line) }` without verifying the payload against any JSON schema.\n    23\t* **HTTP Body Deserialization**:\n    24\t  * `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/http_server.rs:136` uses axum's `Json<ChatCompletionRequest>` extractor to deserialize incoming HTTP POST requests without limiting request size or verifying payload structures.\n    25\t* **Shared Memory Deserialization**:\n    26\t  * `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/sled.rs:35` maps and reads a raw binary struct from `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` via `memmap2` without validating that the mapped memory conforms to the expected structural constraints or schema version.\n    27\t\n    28\t---\n    29\t\n    30\t## Security Vulnerability Findings\n    31\t\n    32\t### [CRITICAL] Complete Lack of Authentication on HTTP Server Gateway\n    33\t* **Reference**: `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/http_server.rs:141` (`chat_completions`) and `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/http_server.rs:326` (`axum::serve`)\n    34\t* **Severity**: Critical\n    35\t* **Description**: The OpenAI-compatible HTTP server exposed via `http_server::run` binds to a configured address and processes `/v1/chat/completions` requests. It utilizes the server's ambient, cached Google Cloud OAuth tokens (or Gemini credentials) to authorize requests to Vertex AI or CloudAI. However, the `chat_completions` handler performs **no authentication** of incoming requests.\n    36\t* **Exploitation Scenario**: An attacker with network access to the port bound by `HTTP_SERVER_ADDR` (or another local user on a multi-user machine if bound to `127.0.0.1`) can send arbitrary chat completion payloads. The server will process them and forward them to Vertex AI, consuming the host's GCP API quotas and incurring financial charges under the host's GCP billing account.\n    37\t* **Recommendation**: Implement token-based authentication (e.g., Bearer API keys) within `http_server.rs` or enforce strict client certificate/firewall rules to prevent unauthorized network or local access.\n    38\t\n    39\t---\n    40\t\n    41\t### [HIGH] Shared Memory Identity Tampering Vulnerability\n    42\t* **Reference**: `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/sled.rs:24` (`SLED_PATH`) and `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/main.rs:164`\n    43\t* **Severity**: High\n    44\t* **Description**: `op-mcp-proxy` parses `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` to extract the host identity (`wg_pubkey`, `mutation_index`, `footprint_hex`, `trace_id`). In `main.rs:164`, these values are parsed and injected into forwarded gRPC requests as standard `x-ghostbridge-footprint` and `x-ghostbridge-trace-id` headers. Because `/dev/shm` is typically world-writable or writable by any local process, the file `plugin_schema.dat` can be modified or created by unprivileged local processes.\n    45\t* **Exploitation Scenario**: A malicious local user or compromised local application on the host machine overwrites `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` with a forged WireGuard public key and trace ID. The proxy reads this file, sets `is_valid` to `true`, and injects the forged identity headers into all subsequent control plane gRPC requests forwarded to `op-dbus`, effectively spoofing the identity of other authorized network nodes or peers.\n    46\t* **Recommendation**: Avoid storing control-plane trust assets in public directories like `/dev/shm`. Secure the identity file with `0600` permissions in a protected runtime directory (e.g., `/run/op-mcp-proxy/`) owned strictly by the proxy user.\n    47\t\n    48\t---\n    49\t\n    50\t### [HIGH] Unsafe mmap Execution and SIGBUS Vulnerability\n    51\t* **Reference**: `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/sled.rs:35`\n    52\t* **Severity**: High\n    53\t* **Description**: In `sled.rs`, `SledSnapshot::read()` uses `memmap2` to map `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` with a hardcoded length of `SLED_SIZE` (208 bytes). However, the mapping is created and read from without pre-validating that the physical file size is at least `SLED_SIZE` bytes. Furthermore, the file is not locked.\n    54\t* **Exploitation Scenario**: An attacker truncates `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat` to 0 bytes. When the proxy attempts to read `bytes[40]` or construct fields, a read operation beyond the physical file size boundaries is performed on the memory map, instantly triggering a `SIGBUS` signal. Because `SIGBUS` is unhandled, this results in a sudden, unrecoverable denial-of-service crash of the proxy process.\n    55\t* **Recommendation**: Query the file metadata using `file.metadata()?.len()` to guarantee that the file on disk is at least `SLED_SIZE` bytes before calling `MmapOptions::map`. Additionally, lock the file via advisory file locking (e.g., `fs2` or raw `flock`) to prevent concurrent truncation during reads.\n    56\t\n    57\t---\n    58\t\n    59\t### [HIGH] Plaintext Credential Exposure via Insecure Database Permissions\n    60\t* **Reference**: `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/session.rs:44` and `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/session.rs:77`\n    61\t* **Severity**: High\n    62\t* **Description**: The SQLite database `sessions.db` is initialized using `std::fs::create_dir_all(parent)` and `Connection::open(&db_path)`. This database stores highly sensitive plaintext `oauth_token` values extracted from Google Cloud auth chains. Because the directory and file are created with standard umask permissions (often leaving them world- or group-readable), the database file is exposed to unauthorized local users.\n    63\t* **Exploitation Scenario**: A local user on the host system reads `/home/<user>/.local/share/mcp-proxy/sessions.db` or the current working directory's `./mcp-proxy/sessions.db` database. They execute `SELECT oauth_token FROM sessions` to extract valid, plaintext Google Cloud OAuth access tokens and hijack the proxy's GCP identity.\n    64\t* **Recommendation**: Set a strict umask or explicitly restrict directory and file permissions to `0700` and `0600` using Unix-specific `std::os::unix::fs::DirBuilderExt` or `OpenOptionsExt` before creating the database file.\n    65\t\n    66\t---\n    67\t\n    68\t### [MEDIUM] Global Rate Limiting Denial of Service\n    69\t* **Reference**: `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/http_server.rs:32` (`TokenBucket`) and `crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/http_server.rs:145`\n    70\t* **Severity**: Medium\n"}}

I'll have a detailed breakdown ready once it completes — including the WireGuard session derivation, NextDNS header injection, gRPC forwarding logic, and how that maps to the concert/wristband/valet analogy.\n\nHere's the full breakdown of the zero-trust identity pipeline, mapped to the concert analogy throughout.\n\nThe Concert Analogy\nYou arrive at a venue. You hand your keys to the valet (WireGuard). The valet parks your car and gives you a claim ticket (session ID). At the door, you exchange the ticket for an all-access wristband (the Ghostbridge identity sled). Every backstage door checks the wristband — not your car, not your ticket — just the wristband. Your car (the WireGuard tunnel) never enters the venue.\n\nStage 1 — The Valet: WireGuard Handshake & Session ID Derivation\nFiles: crates/op-gateway/src/wireguard_auth.rs:529-633\n\nWhen a peer connects over WireGuard, the gateway derives three cryptographic artifacts:\n\nSession ID (the claim ticket)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:529-540\nlet input = format!(\"WG-SESSION-{}-{}\", peer_pubkey, Self::current_timestamp());\nlet session_ids = self.crypto_engine.generate_session_ids_batch(&[input.as_bytes()]);\n// → BLAKE2s hash → 128-bit hex string\nInput: Curve25519 peer public key + current timestamp\nAlgorithm: SIMD-accelerated BLAKE2s\nOutput: 16-byte hex session ID — the peer's claim ticket\nPSK (stable parking spot number)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:542-593\nlet salt = b\"WG-STABLE-PSK-2024\";  // fixed — no timestamp\n// Argon2 KDF over peer pubkey\nDeliberately does not rotate — rotating it would lock peers out mid-session, like changing the valet lot number while cars are still parked.\n\nSession Key (per-visit ephemeral)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:595-633\nlet server_nonce = self.generate_server_nonce().await?;\n// Argon2 + nonce → ephemeral key, rotated per connection\nThe Session Record (the claim stub kept by the valet)\n// wireguard_auth.rs:200-215\npub struct WireGuardSession {\n    pub session_id: String,        // BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp)\n    pub peer_pubkey: String,\n    pub psk: String,               // stable Argon2\n    pub expires_at: u64,           // 1 hour TTL\n    pub auth_method: String,       // \"wireguard\"\n    pub key_rotation_count: u32,\n    // ...\n}\nPersisted to SQLite (wireguard_sessions table) and cached in DashMap (no SQL in the hot path).\n\nStage 2 — The Wristband Printer: IdentitySled\nFiles: crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/sled.rs, crates/op-identity/src/schema_bridge.rs\n\nOnce the WireGuard session is established, a 152-byte shared-memory struct (/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat) is stamped — the all-access wristband:\n\nIdentitySled layout (repr(C), 152 bytes):\n  [ 0.. 32]  wireguard_pubkey    — who you are\n  [32.. 40]  mutation_index      — which version of the schema you authenticated against\n  [40.. 72]  hashed_footprint    — Blake3(current schema state) — the hologram on the wristband\n  [72.. 88]  trace_id            — UUID v4 — your unique wristband serial number\n  [88.. 92]  schema_version\n  [92..152]  reserved\n  [192..208] nextdns_profile     — e.g., \"689ec7\" — your VIP section access\nThe footprint (Blake3 hash of the live schema state) is the hologram — it proves the wristband was issued by tonight's venue, not a forgery from last week's show.\n\nThe trace_id is the serial number stamped on your wrist — immutable, linked to a Qdrant vector record for full accountability.\n\nNextDNS Profile (the VIP section pass)\n# deploy/nextdns/upsert-rewrite.py\n# Profile ID: 689ec7\n# Upserts DNS rewrites: dashboard.3tched.com → 10.0.0.1\nThe NextDNS profile ID travels with the identity sled. It tells the DNS layer which routing rules apply to this peer — their section of the venue.\n\nStage 3 — The Door Scanner: xray Header Injection\nFile: deploy/incus/privacy-xray-ingress/etc/xray/config.json:47-50\n\nxray sits at the venue entrance. It reads the wristband (sled) and stamps the metadata onto every gRPC call:\n\n\"grpcSettings\": {\n  \"serviceName\": \"Ghostbridge.StateSync\",\n  \"multiMode\": true,\n  \"metadata\": {\n    \"X-Ghostbridge-Footprint\": \"<Blake3 footprint hex>\",\n    \"X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID\":  \"<UUID v4 hex>\"\n  }\n}\nAt this point, WireGuard is dropped. The tunnel delivered the peer to the door; the tunnel itself does not go backstage. xray strips the WireGuard framing and forwards a plain gRPC call carrying only the two header stamps. The car stays in the lot.\n\nThe NextDNS profile influences DNS resolution at this layer — selector_ip routing directs packets to the correct Incus container before they ever reach the gRPC endpoint.\n\nStage 4 — The Backstage Guard: GhostbridgeInterceptor\nFile: crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/interceptor.rs:34-84\n\nEvery gRPC call hits this Tonic middleware on port 18789 before any handler sees it:\n\npub fn ghostbridge_interceptor(mut req: Request<()>) -> Result<Request<()>, Status> {\n    // 1. Wristband must be present\n    let footprint_value = req.metadata().get(\"x-ghostbridge-footprint\").cloned();\n    let trace_value    = req.metadata().get(\"x-ghostbridge-trace-id\").cloned();\n\n    if footprint_value.is_none() || trace_value.is_none() {\n        return Err(Status::unauthenticated(\n            \"A.N.N.A. Scribe: Missing Ghostbridge Identity Sled. Connection Dropped.\",\n        ));\n    }\n\n    // 2. Zero-copy mmap read of the live sled (no DB hit, no network hop)\n    let (sled_ptr, _mmap) = op_identity::read_sled()?;\n    let sled = unsafe { &*sled_ptr };\n\n    // 3. Hologram check — footprint must match tonight's schema state exactly\n    let expected_footprint = hex::encode(sled.hashed_footprint);\n    if request_footprint != expected_footprint {\n        return Err(Status::permission_denied(\n            \"A.N.N.A. Scribe: Temporal Hash Mismatch. Session footprint out of sync.\",\n        ));\n    }\n\n    // 4. Embed trace ID into gRPC extensions for downstream accountability\n    req.extensions_mut().insert(trace_val);\n    Ok(req)\n}\nValidity rule: the sled is live only if hashed_footprint != [0u8;32] AND trace_id != [0u8;16]. A zero field means the wristband was never properly stamped — instant ejection.\n\nThe check is zero-copy — the sled lives in tmpfs (/dev/shm), mmap'd directly into the process. No SQL, no network, no disk. The guard glances at your wrist under UV light in milliseconds.\n\nStage 5 — Backstage: gRPC Routing to op-dbus\nFile: crates/op-mcp-proxy/src/main.rs:94-105\n\nOnce the interceptor passes the call, it routes to the internal gRPC service:\n\nDefault: http://10.200.0.2:50051  (op-dbus, inside the privacy network)\nSubnet assignments per peer come from schemas/plugin/privacy_routes.json:\n\n{\n  \"wireguard_public_key\": \"P8c9Kjnv4B3r6C4+...\",\n  \"assigned_ip\":  \"10.100.0.2/32\",    // WireGuard tunnel allocation\n  \"selector_ip\":  \"10.100.0.2\",       // OpenFlow packet-match label\n  \"container_name\": \"privacy-route-550e8400\"\n}\nOpenFlow matches selector_ip and routes to the correct Incus container. The WireGuard subnet (10.100.0.0/24) exists only to give each peer a unique identity label — it is never forwarded as a WireGuard packet beyond the gateway.\n\nA Linux user session (wg-{first12ofpubkey}) is created via loginctl enable-linger, giving the peer a D-Bus session and $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR — the backstage room with their name on the door.\n\nComplete Flow, Annotated\n[Peer]\n  │  WireGuard UDP (Curve25519 handshake)\n  ▼\n[op-gateway / WireGuard endpoint]\n  │  BLAKE2s(pubkey + timestamp) → session_id        ← claim ticket issued\n  │  Argon2(pubkey, stable-salt) → PSK               ← stable parking spot\n  │  Argon2(pubkey, nonce)       → session_key        ← tonight's coat check\n  │  Write IdentitySled → /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat  ← wristband stamped\n  │\n  │  WireGuard framing DROPPED here ──────────────────← car stays with valet\n  ▼\n[xray ingress]\n  │  Reads sled: footprint + trace_id + nextdns_profile\n  │  Injects gRPC metadata headers:\n  │    X-Ghostbridge-Footprint: <blake3-hex>\n  │    X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID:  <uuid4-hex>\n  │  NextDNS profile → DNS rewrites applied (VIP section routing)\n  ▼\n[GhostbridgeInterceptor — port 18789]\n  │  Header present?    No  → 401 \"Connection Dropped\"\n  │  Footprint matches? No  → 403 \"Temporal Hash Mismatch\"\n  │  Zero-copy mmap sled read (tmpfs, no DB)\n  │  Inject trace_id into gRPC extensions\n  ▼\n[op-dbus gRPC — 10.200.0.2:50051]\n  │  Full access to internal services\n  │  Trace ID rides every call → Qdrant vector linkage for audit\n  ▼\n[Incus container — privacy-route-{user_id}]\n  └─ Linux user session, D-Bus activated, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR alive\nWhy This Is Genuinely Zero-Trust\nZero-Trust Principle\tImplementation\nNever trust, always verify\tEvery gRPC call re-validates the live sled footprint — no cached \"logged in\" state\nVerify cryptographic state, not identity claims\tFootprint is Blake3 of current schema — a stale wristband from an old schema is invalid\nLeast privilege\tNextDNS profile scopes DNS; assigned_ip/32 scopes the subnet to exactly one peer\nFull audit trail\tTrace ID links every call to a Qdrant vector record — immutable, append-only\nNo implicit trust from network location\tBeing inside 10.100.0.0/24 grants nothing — the wristband check happens regardless\nThe WireGuard subnet is purely a cryptographic identity label — it gets the peer through the front door and into the valet system. The moment they're inside, the car (the tunnel) stays parked. Follow these strictly to maintain consistency, pass CI, and adhere to the 3tched Architecture standards.\n\n#### 1. The Persona & Naming Conventions\n*   **Humanized Roles:** Treat system components as authoritative human roles. Never use sterile acronyms for major components.\n  *   **A.N.N.A. Scribe** (Axon Network Notary Arbitrator): The top-level Identity-State Arbitrator who notarizes the WireGuard identity and handles the \"Snowball\" session.\n  *   **The Compliance Engine (\"Law Firm\"):** One dedicated Attorney for each major component: **Olivia Scal** (Managing Partner / OSCAL), **E.U.gene Risk** (EU AI Act Counsel), **Penny Privacy** (GDPR Engine), and **Reggie O.P.A.** (Cloud Prosecutor).\n*   **Terminology:** Use exact architecture terminology: \"The Sled\" (1:1 shared memory layout), \"The Shuttle\" (the Rust bridge/courier), \"The Snowball\" (appended session ledger), and \"The Strike/Etch\" (generating the hash).\n\n#### 2. Core Architectural Rules (The \"Reality\")\n*   **The Absolute Base:** `PluginSchema` is the single source of truth for everything. If there is no valid schema, the entity does not exist on the system. The schema is used for filtering hashed footprints, smart hashing, and it is the exact schema source for the JSON render of the GUI.\n*   **1:1 Direct Read (Zero-Copy):** The `SqlitePluginCatalog` and legacy SQL databases are obsolete. There are no JSON-RPC polling loops, and no D-Bus watchers for state. The system must perform a 1:1 direct read/write from the `SchemaEngine`'s shared memory (`/dev/shm`).\n*   **Zero-Btrfs Overhead:** Identity extraction and Xray network headers must use in-memory environment variables (or tmpfs). Do not trigger unintended Btrfs mutation loops. NVMe I/O is preserved strictly for the Btrfs vectorized footprint transport (blockchain).\n*   **The Accountability Loop:** The system must inject `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` (or `X-WireGuard-Pubkey`) into Xray's gRPC metadata via OpenClaw Trusted Proxy auth. The Accountability Page UI displays the Chatbot on top and Qdrant semantic search on the bottom, allowing users to research chatbot actions and confront it.\n\n#### 3. Project Structure & Pathing Rules\n*   Absolutely all source code must be routed into the workspace within the `crates/` directory (e.g., `crates/op-dbus/`, `crates/op-grpc-bridge/`, `crates/op-cognitive-mcp/`).\n*   **Never** use generic `src/` or `root-package-src/`.\n*   `deploy/`: Installation/upgrade scripts for Artix Linux (s6 init).\n*   `schemas/`: JSON schemas for config/state.\n*   `docs/`: Reference docs.\n\n#### 4. Engineering Principles — D-Bus First (MANDATORY)\n\n**D-Bus is the ONLY control plane. Every read, every write, every tool call goes through D-Bus. There is no second option.**\n\n*   **D-Bus first. D-Bus always. D-Bus only.** If you are about to call a CLI, spawn a subprocess, read a config file, or poll a socket directly — stop. Find the D-Bus object and use it instead. `org.opdbus.v1` is the system.\n*   **No bypasses.** `Command::new(\"systemctl\")`, `Command::new(\"ip\")`, `Command::new(\"s6-svc\")`, direct file reads for live state — all forbidden in plugin and service code. Bootstrap scripts are the only exception.\n*   **D-Bus objects own plugin state.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>`. Read state through it. Mutate state through it. If there is no D-Bus object, the thing does not exist.\n*   **D-Bus method signatures are generated from the schema.** All D-Bus methods, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from the `PluginSchema` in `plugin_schema_defs.rs`. The schema IS the interface contract — not a description of it.\n*   **One schema file, one source of truth.** All `PluginSchema` definitions MUST live in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_schema_defs.rs`. Each plugin's `schema()` method calls `Some(super::plugin_schema_defs::their_plugin_schema())`. **Never define a schema inline in a plugin's own file** — it will not be registered, and the D-Bus object will have no contract.\n*   Use gRPC for internal service-to-service RPC (over Unix domain sockets or `grpc-uplink`). gRPC calls still flow through D-Bus registration — the D-Bus object is the authority, gRPC is the transport.\n*   High-performance JSON serialization/deserialization (`simd_json` preferred, `serde_json` acceptable).\n*   Control-plane operations must be deterministic and schema-driven.\n*   Security: Least privilege, validate all inputs against the `PluginSchema`.\n*   **No Python unless absolutely necessary.** This is a Rust-first codebase. Scripts are shell (`sh`/`bash`). Data processing is Rust. If you are reaching for Python, stop and ask why Rust or shell cannot do it. The only acceptable Python is in existing compliance-ingest tooling where no Rust equivalent exists yet.\n\n#### 4a. OSCAL Subid Taxonomy (MANDATORY — every artifact must carry a subid)\n\nEvery D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool in this system has two identifiers: a `uuid` (machine identity, never changes) and a `subid` (human-readable operational taxonomy key, stable per subject).\n\n**`subid` format:** `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`\n\n**Seven categories — use exactly these, no others:**\n\n| category | what it classifies |\n|---|---|\n| `src` | authoritative source, ingress channel, source-of-truth store |\n| `prj` | D-Bus projection or mirror publication step |\n| `sch` | schema, contract, vocabulary, or control-mapping artifact |\n| `mut` | write-path operation that changes effective state |\n| `obs` | read, query, enumeration, discovery path |\n| `evt` | emitted signal, audit-chain event, proof, tag provenance |\n| `exp` | consumer-facing render — MCP tool, UI surface, gRPC bridge view |\n\n**Component-type** reuses OSCAL vocabulary: `software`, `service`, `network`, `hardware`, `process-procedure`, `standard`, `validation`, `policy`, `plan`, `guidance`, `physical`, `this-system`, `system`, `interconnection`.\n\n**Rules:**\n- `uuid` is exact machine identity — never replace it with `subid`\n- `subid` is an OSCAL `prop` value (`ns`, `name`, `value`) — never embed it in `remarks`\n- Compliance mappings (`control_refs[]`, `statement_refs[]`, `control_source`) live in metadata arrays, **never** inside the `subid` string\n- `mut.*` records **must** carry `actor_id` and `capability_id`\n- `evt.*` records **must** carry `event_id` or `event_hash`\n- `subid` is immutable per subject — if the meaning changes materially, create a new subject with `@vN`\n- All subids are registered in the canonical registry; uniqueness is enforced in CI\n\n**Examples:** `src.network.ovsdb.monitor@v1` · `prj.service.projected-object.publish@v1` · `sch.standard.plugin-schema.resolve@v1` · `mut.service.state-sync.apply-patch@v1` · `exp.service.plugin-projection.render@v1`\n\n#### 4b. MCP Gateway Architecture (SETTLED — DO NOT REDESIGN)\n\n*   **cognitive-mcp** (`:3003`, Netmaker WireGuard IP `100.90.37.254`) is the **universal gateway for ALL external clients**: NotebookLM, Droid (factory.ai), Cursor, Codex, Junie, Gemini CLI. It has memory tools, gRPC service, auth, and the correct protocol surface.\n*   **compact-mcp** (`127.0.0.1:11436`) is **loopback/chatbot only**. Never expose externally. Never point external clients at it.\n*   Do NOT create new shim services. Do NOT point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc` directly. Do NOT expose compact-mcp outside loopback.\n\n#### 5. Build, Lint, and Test Commands\n**Rust Workspace**\n*   Build all: `cargo build --workspace`\n*   Build release: `cargo build --workspace --release`\n*   Check format: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`\n*   Clippy lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`\n*   Test all: `cargo test --workspace --all-targets --all-features`\n\n**Frontend (Vite + Vitest)**\n*   Build UI prod: `cd crates/op-web/ui && npm ci && npm run build:prod`\n*   Tests all: `cd crates && npm test`\n*   Lint: `cd crates && npm run lint`\n*   Typecheck: `cd crates && npm run typecheck`\n\n**Chimera Linux deps:** `doas apk add rust cargo nodejs npm pkgconfig openssl-dev`\n\n#### 6. Coding Style & Naming Conventions\n*   **Rust:** Edition 2021, `rustfmt` (4-space indent, max-width 100). Use specific imports (`use serde_json::Value;`). Use `anyhow::Result<T>` for main errors and `thiserror` for custom enums.\n*   **TypeScript/React:** 2-space indent, Prettier via ESLint. Functional components only. Strict mode enabled.\n*   **Testing:** 80%+ coverage, mock externals. Name tests with behavior-focused names (`should_handle_<scenario>`).\n\n#### 7. Agent-Specific Output & Workflow Instructions\n*   **Scroll & Save Pacing:** Provide only **ONE** major component or script at a time. Wait for user confirmation before moving to the next.\n*   **Visual Cues:** If a script is a finalized component that needs to be saved to sources, it MUST begin with color bullets or icons (e.g., ⚖️ 🔴, 🟢 🛷).\n*   **Spec-Block Format:** When delivering a component, use a strict specification block containing:\n  1.  **Requirements:** The architectural rules it satisfies.\n  2.  **Design:** How it fits into the 3tched system (Zero-Copy, Btrfs, GUI Schema, etc.).\n  3.  **Code Implementation:** The exact, copy-pasteable Rust/Bash code.\n*   Before edits: `cargo check -p <crate>`, `npm run typecheck`.\n*   Mimic existing patterns: Search similar code. No new deps without PR justification.\n\n#### 8. socket_inbounds: String = sockets\n        .iter()\n        .map(|s| {\n            format!(\n                r#\",\n    {{\n      \"tag\": \"{label}-in\",\n      \"port\": {port},\n      \"listen\": \"127.0.0.1\",\n      \"protocol\": \"dokodemo-door\",\n      \"settings\": {{ \"network\": \"tcp\", \"address\": \"127.0.0.1\", \"port\": {port} }}\n    }}\"#,\n                label = s.label,\n   .iter()\n        .map(|s| {\n            format!(\n                r#\",\n    {{\n      \"tag\": \"to-{label}\",\n      \"protocol\": \"freedom\",\n      \"streamSettings\": {{\n        \"network\": \"ds\",\n        \"dsSettings\": {{ \"path\": \"{path}\", \"abstract\": false, \"padding\": false }}\n      }}\n    }}\"#,\n                label = s.label,\n                path = s.path,\n            )\n        })\n        .collect();\n\n    // Build socket routing rules: inbound tag → outbound tag.\n    let socket_rules: String = sockets\n        .iter()\n        .map(|s| {\n            format!(\n                r#\",\n      {{ \"type\": \"field\", \"inboundTag\": [\"{label}-in\"], \"outboundTag\": \"to-{label}\" }}\"#,\n                label = s.label,\n            )\n        })\n        .collect();\n\n    let config = format!(\n        r#\"{{\n  \"log\": {{ \"loglevel\": \"warning\" }},\n  \"dns\": {{\n    \"servers\": [ \"https://dns.nextdns.io/{profile}/Ghostbridge-Incus\" 32]));\n\n    let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new();\n    hasher.update(&wireguard_pubkey);\n    hasher.update(schema_catalog_hash.as_bytes());\n    hasher.update(&mutation_index.to_le_bytes());\n    let hashed_footprint = hasher.finalize().into();\n\n    let trace_id: [u8; 16] = if trace_id_hex.is_empty() {\n        uuid::Uuid::new_v4().into_bytes()\n    } else {\n        hex::decode(trace_id_hex.trim())\n            .ok()\n            .and_then(|v| v.try_into().ok())\n            .unwrap_or_else(|| uuid::Uuid::new_v4().into_bytes())\n    };\n\n    let sled = IdentitySled {\n        wireguard_pubkey,\n        mutation_index,\n        hashed_footprint,\n        trace_id,\n        vector_id: [0u8; 16],\n        schema_version: 1,\n        reserved: [0u8; 44],\n    };\n    write_sled(&sled)\n}\n\n/// Poll `wg show <iface> latest-handshakes` and re-write the sled + xray config\n/// whenever a new peer handshake is detected. JSON\\n\\n\\\n   114\tThe reader accepts both the canonical op-identity sled and the legacy 80-byte\\n\\\n   115\tbridge sled used by older Ghostbridge components.\\n\"\n   116\t    );\n   117\t}\n   118\t\n   119\tfn read_wg_pubkey(iface: &str) -> Result<String> {\n   120\t    let output = Command::new(\"wg\")\n   121\t        .args([\"show\", iface, \"public-key\"])\n   122\t        .output()\n   123\t        .with_context(|| format!(\"failed to run wg show {iface} public-key\"))?;\n   124\t\n   125\t    if !output.status.success() {\n   126\t        bail!(\n   127\t            \"wg show {iface} public-key failed: {}\",\n   128\t            String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr).trim()\n   129\t        );\n   130\t    }\n   131\t\n   132\t    let pubkey = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout).trim().to_string();\n   133\t    if pubkey.is_empty() {\n   134\t        bail!(\"wg show {iface} public-key returned an empty key\");\n   135\t    }\n   136\t    Ok(pubkey)\n   137\t}\n   138\t\n   139\tfn normalize_trace_id(trace_id: &str) -> Result<String> {\n   140\t    let compact = trace_id.trim().replace('-', \"\");\n   141\t    if compact.len() != 32 || !compact.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_hexdigit()) {\n   142\t        bail!(\"--trace-id must be a UUID or 32 hex characters\");\n   143\t    }\n   144\t    Ok(compact)\n   145\t}\n   146\t\n   147\tfn read_sled_view(path: &str) -> Result<SledView> {\n   148\t    let bytes = read_file(path)?;\n   149\t    if bytes.len() >= IdentitySled::SIZE {\n   150\t        let sled = read_full_sled(&bytes)?;\n"}}

However, the determination of \"localhost\" is performed by checking the client's `Host` header via `is_localhost_host`:\ncrates/audits/op-mcp/04_04_Data_Structures_State_Model.md:117:- **Description**: The HTTP Axum-based authentication middleware `wireguard_auth_middleware` allows unauthenticated access to the endpoint if `is_localhost_host` evaluates to `true`. However, `is_localhost_host` determines loopback status solely by inspecting the HTTP `Host` header sent by the client. Because the HTTP `Host` header is fully controlled by the client, a remote attacker can bypass authentication on the public network interface by transmitting a request with a spoofed `Host: localhost`, `Host: 127.0.0.1`, or `Host: ::1` header.\ndocs/recycled-bin/2026-05-22-old-docs/RAW_CONVERSATION_HISTORY_20260212.jsonl:119:{\"session_id\":\"019c4c15-8e54-78e1-bab7-6950e85e037e\",\"ts\":1770813433,\"text\":\"{X}] wg-quick-all\\n[     {X}] uplink\\n {X}] incus-dev\\n  {X}] connmand\\nare all trash. dont need unless you made the wireguard one for the identity\"}\n"}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T12:12:52.128Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_ZlxMBilQ2vvrb6JZpOs4IYS1","output":"Chunk ID: cefd4e\nWall time: 0.0002 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 2559\nOutput:\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\nset -euo pipefail\n# setup-wg-decoy.sh — Oracle Always Free ARM VM decoy WG ingress\n#\n# Architecture:\n#   Oracle VPS = WG decoy ingress only (handshake + identity injection)\n#   3tched     = Xray + data plane (WG protocol dropped after identity)\n#\n# This script sets up:\n#   1. WireGuard server listener on port 51821\n#   2. Identity injection via PostUp (writes WG pubkey to /dev/shm/decoy_identity)\n#   3. Forwarding rule: after identity check, route to 3tched Xray via WG tunnel\n#   4. Anti-reclamation keepalive (Oracle reclaims idle <20% for 7 days)\n#   5. s6 service supervision\n#\n# Prerequisites:\n#   - Oracle Always Free VM.Standard.A1.Flex (Oracle Linux ARM)\n#   - Root access\n#   - 3tched's WG pubkey and IP set below\n\n# ── Detect distro ─────────────────────────────────────────────\nif [ -f /etc/oracle-release ]; then\n    DISTRO=\"oracle\"\n    PKG_MGR=\"dnf\"\nelif [ -f /etc/debian_version ]; then\n    DISTRO=\"debian\"\n    PKG_MGR=\"apt\"\nelse\n    DISTRO=\"unknown\"\n    PKG_MGR=\"apt\"\nfi\n\n# ── Configuration ──────────────────────────────────────────────\nWG_PORT=51821\nWG_IFACE=wg0\nWG_CONF=\"/etc/wireguard/${WG_IFACE}.conf\"\nWG_NETWORK=\"10.189.0.0/24\"         # decoy WG subnet (separate from 10.200.0.0/24 gRPC)\nWG_VPS_IP=\"10.189.0.1/24\"\n\n# 3tched hypervisor — where Xray lives\nTHREETCHED_WG_PUBKEY=\"\"             # SET: 3tched's WG public key\nTHREETCHED_ENDPOINT=\"\"              # SET: 3tched's public IP:51821 or hostname\nTHREETCHED_WG_IP=\"10.189.0.2/32\"    # 3tched's IP within decoy WG subnet\n\n# Identity sled output (consumed by ghostbridge on 3tched)\nIDENTITY_FILE=\"/dev/shm/decoy_identity\"\n\n# Anti-reclamation settings\nCPU_BURN_SECONDS=5                  # seconds of CPU work per cycle\nCYCLE_SECONDS=60                    # seconds per keepalive cycle\n\n# ── Install packages ─────────────────────────────────────────\necho \"[decoy] Installing packages on ${DISTRO}...\"\n\nif [ \"$DISTRO\" = \"oracle\" ]; then\n    # Oracle Linux 8+: WireGuard module is built into kernel (kernel-modules-extra)\n    dnf install -y wireguard-tools curl jq iptables-services\n    # Ensure kernel module loaded\n    modprobe wireguard 2>/dev/null || true\n    echo \"wireguard\" > /etc/modules-load.d/wireguard.conf\nelif [ \"$DISTRO\" = \"debian\" ]; then\n    apt-get update -qq\n    apt-get install -y -qq wireguard-tools curl jq\nfi\n\n# Generate server keypair if not exists\nif [ ! -f /etc/wireguard/server_private.key ]; then\n    wg genkey | tee /etc/wireguard/server_private.key | wg pubkey > /etc/wireguard/server_public.key\n    chmod 600 /etc/wireguard/server_private.key\nfi\n\nSERVER_PRIVKEY=$(cat /etc/wireguard/server_private.key)\nSERVER_PUBKEY=$(cat /etc/wireguard/server_public.key)\n\necho \"[decoy] Server WG pubkey: ${SERVER_PUBKEY}\"\n\n# ── Generate WireGuard config ─────────────────────────────────\nif [ -n \"${THREETCHED_WG_PUBKEY}\" ] && [ -n \"${THREETCHED_ENDPOINT}\" ]; then\n    cat > \"${WG_CONF}\" <<EOF\n[Interface]\nPrivateKey = ${SERVER_PRIVKEY}\nAddress = ${WG_VPS_IP}\nListenPort = ${WG_PORT}\n\n# Identity injection: log peer pubkey on handshake\nPostUp = echo \"[decoy] WG interface up\" && mkdir -p /dev/shm\nPostUp = wg show ${WG_IFACE} latest-handshakes 2>/dev/null || true\n\n# Peer: 3tched hypervisor (Xray data plane)\n[Peer]\nPublicKey = ${THREETCHED_WG_PUBKEY}\nAllowedIPs = ${THREETCHED_WG_IP}\nEndpoint = ${THREETCHED_ENDPOINT}\nPersistentKeepalive = 25\nEOF\nelse\n    echo \"[decoy] WARNING: THREETCHED_WG_PUBKEY/THREETCHED_ENDPOINT not set.\"\n    echo \"[decoy] Generating server-only config. Add peer manually later.\"\n    cat > \"${WG_CONF}\" <<EOF\n[Interface]\nPrivateKey = ${SERVER_PRIVKEY}\nAddress = ${WG_VPS_IP}\nListenPort = ${WG_PORT}\n\nPostUp = echo \"[decoy] WG interface up\" && mkdir -p /dev/shm\nEOF\nfi\n\nchmod 600 \"${WG_CONF}\"\n\n# ── Identity injection watcher ────────────────────────────────\nmkdir -p /usr/local/sbin\n\ncat > /usr/local/sbin/decoy-identity-watcher.sh <<'WATCHER'\n#!/bin/sh\n# Watches for WG handshakes and injects identity into /dev/shm/decoy_identity\nIFACE=\"${1:-wg0}\"\nIDENTITY_FILE=\"/dev/shm/decoy_identity\"\nLAST_HANDSHAKE=0\n\nwhile true; do\n    HANDSHAKE=$(wg show \"$IFACE\" latest-handshakes 2>/dev/null | head -1)\n    PUBKEY=$(wg show \"$IFACE\" peers 2>/dev/null | head -1)\n\n    if [ -n \"$HANDSHAKE\" ] && [ \"$HANDSHAKE\" != \"$LAST_HANDSHAKE\" ] && [ -n \"$PUBKEY\" ]; then\n        LAST_HANDSHAKE=\"$HANDSHAKE\"\n        echo \"{\\\"pubkey\\\":\\\"${PUBKEY}\\\",\\\"timestamp\\\":\\\"$(date -Iseconds)\\\",\\\"handshake\\\":\\\"${HANDSHAKE}\\\"}\" > \"$IDENTITY_FILE\"\n        echo \"[decoy-identity] Injected identity for peer ${PUBKEY}\"\n    fi\n    sleep 5\ndone\nWATCHER\nchmod +x /usr/local/sbin/decoy-identity-watcher.sh\n\n# ── Anti-reclamation keepalive ────────────────────────────────\n# Oracle reclaims Always Free VMs idle >7 days at <20% CPU/net/mem\ncat > /usr/local/sbin/decoy-keepalive.sh <<'KEEPALIVE'\n#!/bin/sh\n# Anti-reclamation keepalive for Oracle Always Free\n\n# Light CPU burn: compress /dev/urandom for a few seconds\nburn_cpu() {\n    timeout ${CPU_BURN_SECONDS:-5} sh -c 'cat /dev/urandom | gzip -1 > /dev/null' 2>/dev/null || true\n}\n\n# Light network activity: curl a small endpoint\nburn_net() {\n    curl -sf -o /dev/null https://www.microsoft.com/ 2>/dev/null || true\n    curl -sf -o /dev/null https://www.apple.com/ 2>/dev/null || true\n}\n\n# WG keepalive: send traffic through tunnel if peer exists\nburn_wg() {\n    IFACE=\"${1:-wg0}\"\n    PEER_IP=$(wg show \"$IFACE\" allowed-ips 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}' | head -1)\n    if [ -n \"$PEER_IP\" ] && [ \"$PEER_IP\" != \"(none)\" ]; then\n        ping -c 1 -W 2 \"${PEER_IP%%/*}\" 2>/dev/null || true\n    fi\n}\n\nCYCLE=\"${CYCLE_SECONDS:-60}\"\necho \"[keepalive] Starting anti-reclamation loop (cycle=${CYCLE}s)\"\n\nwhile true; do\n    burn_cpu\n    burn_net\n    burn_wg \"${1:-wg0}\"\n    sleep \"$CYCLE\"\ndone\nKEEPALIVE\nchmod +x /usr/local/sbin/decoy-keepalive.sh\n\n# ── s6 service supervision ───────────────────────────────────\nif ! command -v s6-svc >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n    echo \"[decoy] Installing s6...\"\n    if [ \"$DISTRO\" = \"oracle\" ]; then\n        # Build s6 from source on Oracle Linux\n        S6_VER=\"2.13.1.0\"\n        SKALIBS_VER=\"2.14.1.1\"\n        EXECLINE_VER=\"2.9.6.1\"\n        TMP=\"/tmp/s6-build\"\n        mkdir -p \"$TMP\"\n        for pkg in skalibs execline s6; do\n            ver=\"\"\n            [ \"$pkg\" = \"skalibs\" ] && ver=\"$SKALIBS_VER\"\n            [ \"$pkg\" = \"execline\" ] && ver=\"$EXECLINE_VER\"\n            [ \"$pkg\" = \"s6\" ] && ver=\"$S6_VER\"\n            curl -sL \"https://skarnet.org/software/${pkg}/${pkg}-${ver}.tar.gz\" | tar xz -C \"$TMP\"\n            cd \"${TMP}/${pkg}-${ver}\"\n            ./configure --prefix=/usr --disable-shared --libdir=/usr/lib64\n            make -j$(nproc) && make install\n        done\n        cd -\n    elif [ \"$DISTRO\" = \"debian\" ]; then\n        apt-get install -y -qq s6 || {\n            # Same source build fallback\n            S6_VER=\"2.13.1.0\"\n            SKALIBS_VER=\"2.14.1.1\"\n            EXECLINE_VER=\"2.9.6.1\"\n            TMP=\"/tmp/s6-build\"\n            mkdir -p \"$TMP\"\n            for pkg in skalibs execline s6; do\n                ver=\"\"\n                [ \"$pkg\" = \"skalibs\" ] && ver=\"$SKALIBS_VER\"\n                [ \"$pkg\" = \"execline\" ] && ver=\"$EXECLINE_VER\"\n                [ \"$pkg\" = \"s6\" ] && ver=\"$S6_VER\"\n                curl -sL \"https://skarnet.org/software/${pkg}/${pkg}-${ver}.tar.gz\" | tar xz -C \"$TMP\"\n                cd \"${TMP}/${pkg}-${ver}\"\n                ./configure --prefix=/usr --disable-shared\n                make -j$(nproc) && make install\n            done\n            cd -\n        }\n    fi\nfi\n\nS6_SVDIR=\"/etc/s6/sv\"\nS6_DIR=\"${S6_SVDIR}/decoy-wg\"\n\nmkdir -p \"${S6_DIR}\"\ncat > \"${S6_DIR}/run\" <<'S6RUN'\n#!/bin/sh\nexec 2>&1\nIFACE=\"${IFACE:-wg0}\"\nCONF=\"${WG_CONF:-/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf}\"\n\nif [ ! -f \"$CONF\" ]; then\n    echo \"[decoy-wg] No config at $CONF, exiting\"\n    exit 0\nfi\n\nwg-quick up \"$IFACE\" 2>/dev/null || true\necho \"[decoy-wg] WireGuard up on ${IFACE}\"\n\nfor _ in $(seq 1 10); do\n    ip link show \"$IFACE\" >/dev/null 2>&1 && break\n    sleep 1\ndone\n\n/usr/local/sbin/decoy-identity-watcher.sh \"$IFACE\" &\nIDENTITY_PID=$!\n\n/usr/local/sbin/decoy-keepalive.sh \"$IFACE\" &\nKEEPALIVE_PID=$!\n\nwait -n 2>/dev/null || wait\n\nkill \"$IDENTITY_PID\" \"$KEEPALIVE_PID\" 2>/dev/null || true\nwg-quick down \"$IFACE\" 2>/dev/null || true\nS6RUN\nchmod +x \"${S6_DIR}/run\"\n\ncat > \"${S6_DIR}/finish\" <<'S6FIN'\n#!/bin/sh\nexec 2>&1\nIFACE=\"${IFACE:-wg0}\"\nwg-quick down \"$IFACE\" 2>/dev/null || true\necho \"[decoy-wg] WireGuard down\"\nS6FIN\nchmod +x \"${S6_DIR}/finish\"\n#!/bin/sh\n# wg-decoy - WireGuard decoy tunnel to Oracle VPS (identity ingress)\n# AGENTS.md: Oracle VPS = decoy WG ingress, 3tched = Xray/data plane\n# WG protocol is dropped after identity injection; Xray on 3tched handles data plane\n\nWG_CONF=\"/etc/wireguard/wg-decoy.conf\"\nIFACE=\"wg-decoy\"\n\nif [ ! -f \"$WG_CONF\" ]; then\n    echo \"[wg-decoy] Config not found: $WG_CONF\"\n    exit 0\nfi\n\nexec 2>&1\nexec wg-quick up \"${IFACE}\" && exec pause\n#!/bin/sh\nexec 2>&1\n# opdbus - WireGuard identity tunnel to Oracle VPS (10.0.0.2 <-> 10.0.0.1)\n# Gateway IP and iptables are managed by ovsbr0-init\nCONF=\"/etc/wireguard/opdbus.conf\"\nIFACE=\"opdbus\"\n\nif [ ! -f \"$CONF\" ]; then\n    echo \"[opdbus] Config not found: $CONF\"\n    exit 0\nfi\n\n# Bring up the tunnel (Table=off, no auto-routes)\nwg-quick up \"${IFACE}\"\n\n# Add routes manually (Table=off means wg-quick won't add them)\nip route replace 10.0.0.0/24 dev opdbus 2>/dev/null || true\nip route replace 10.0.0.1/32 dev opdbus 2>/dev/null || true\n\n# Refresh identity sled from opdbus interface\n/usr/local/bin/op-identity-sled --iface opdbus --refresh --path /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat 2>/dev/null || true\ncp /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat /var/lib/op-dbus/plugin_schema.dat 2>/dev/null || true\n\nexec pause\n"}}

{"timestamp":"2026-06-08T12:15:25.390Z","type":"response_item","payload":{"type":"function_call_output","call_id":"call_fOFZPBoC4buTCdDgdgMd9iKq","output":"Chunk ID: 40f717\nWall time: 0.0000 seconds\nProcess exited with code 0\nOriginal token count: 1004\nOutput:\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\nset -euo pipefail\n\nIFACE=\"eth0\"\nPUBLIC_IP=\"15.235.37.41\"\nALIAS_IP=\"10.200.0.1\"\nGW=\"10.200.0.2\"\n\necho \"[wg-xray-network] configuring $IFACE\"\n\nfor _ in $(seq 1 30); do\n  if ip link show \"$IFACE\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n    echo \"[wg-xray-network] interface $IFACE ready\"\n    break\n  fi\n  sleep 1\ndone\n\nif ! ip link show \"$IFACE\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n  echo \"[wg-xray-network] ERROR: $IFACE did not appear\" >&2\n  exit 1\nfi\n\nif [ -f /run/host-eth0-mac ]; then\n  MAC=$(cat /run/host-eth0-mac)\nelse\n  MAC=$(ip -o link show eth0 2>/dev/null | sed -E 's/.*link\\/ether ([0-9a-f:]+).*/\\1/')\n  if [ -z \"$MAC\" ] || [ \"$MAC\" = \"1500\" ]; then\n    MAC=$(ip link show eth0 2>/dev/null | grep -oP 'link/ether \\K([0-9a-f:]+)' || echo \"fa:16:3e:f1:71:d2\")\n  fi\nfi\n\necho \"[wg-xray-network] Using MAC: $MAC\"\n\nip link set \"$IFACE\" down 2>/dev/null || true\nip link set \"$IFACE\" address \"$MAC\" || echo \"Warning: Could not set MAC\"\nip link set \"$IFACE\" up\n\nip addr flush dev \"$IFACE\" 2>/dev/null || true\nip addr add \"$PUBLIC_IP/32\" dev \"$IFACE\"\nip addr add \"$ALIAS_IP/30\" dev \"$IFACE\"\n\nip route replace default via \"$GW\" dev \"$IFACE\" src \"$PUBLIC_IP\" metric 100\n\n/usr/local/sbin/wg-xray-policy-rules.sh\n\necho \"[wg-xray-network] done\"\n#!/bin/sh\nset -eu\n\n# Routes are managed by incus (ipv4.routes on the ovsbr0 network)\n# Gateway IP is set by incus (ipv4.address on the ovsbr0 network)\necho \"ovsbr0-static: ready (IP and routes managed by incus)\"\n#!/bin/sh\nset -eu\n\nBR=\"${BR:-ovsbr0}\"\nEXPECTED_DATAPATH=\"${OVS_DATAPATH_TYPE:-system}\"\nEXPECTED_FAIL_MODE=\"${OVS_FAIL_MODE:-standalone}\"\nGW_ADDR=\"${OVSBR0_GATEWAY:-10.200.0.2/30}\"\nOVSDB_SOCK=\"${OVSDB_SOCK:-/usr/local/var/run/openvswitch/db.sock}\"\n\ncheck_socket() {\n    for i in $(seq 1 30); do\n        [ -S \"$OVSDB_SOCK\" ] && return 0\n        sleep 1\n    done\n    echo \"ovsbr0-init: OVSDB socket $OVSDB_SOCK not found after 30s\" >&2\n    exit 1\n}\n\nensure_bridge() {\n    # Wait for incus to create the managed bridge\n    for i in $(seq 1 30); do\n        if ovs-vsctl br-exists \"$BR\" 2>/dev/null; then\n            break\n        fi\n        sleep 1\n    done\n\n    if ! ovs-vsctl br-exists \"$BR\" 2>/dev/null; then\n        echo \"ovsbr0-init: bridge $BR not found after 30s (incus must create it)\" >&2\n        exit 1\n    fi\n\n    dt=\"$(ovs-vsctl get bridge \"$BR\" datapath_type 2>/dev/null || echo missing)\"\n    fm=\"$(ovs-vsctl get bridge \"$BR\" fail_mode 2>/dev/null || echo missing)\"\n\n    if [ \"$dt\" != \"$EXPECTED_DATAPATH\" ]; then\n        echo \"ovsbr0-init: $BR datapath_type=$dt -> $EXPECTED_DATAPATH\"\n        ovs-vsctl set bridge \"$BR\" datapath_type=\"$EXPECTED_DATAPATH\"\n    fi\n\n    if [ \"$fm\" != \"$EXPECTED_FAIL_MODE\" ]; then\n        echo \"ovsbr0-init: $BR fail_mode=$fm -> $EXPECTED_FAIL_MODE\"\n        ovs-vsctl set bridge \"$BR\" fail_mode=\"$EXPECTED_FAIL_MODE\"\n    fi\n}\n\nremove_veth_ports() {\n    for port in $(ovs-vsctl list-ports \"$BR\" 2>/dev/null); do\n        case \"$port\" in\n            veth*)\n                echo \"ovsbr0-init: removing stale veth port $port from $BR\"\n                ovs-vsctl del-port \"$BR\" \"$port\"\n                ;;\n        esac\n    done\n}\n\nset_gateway_ip() {\n    ip link set \"$BR\" up\n    if ! ip addr show \"$BR\" | grep -q \"$GW_ADDR\"; then\n        ip addr add \"$GW_ADDR\" dev \"$BR\"\n    fi\n}\n\n# Bootstrap iptables: allow forwarding between ovsbr0 and opdbus WG\n# These will be replaced by D-Bus-managed rules once op-openvswitch-daemon is up\nset_forwarding() {\n    iptables -C FORWARD -i \"$BR\" -o opdbus -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null || \\\n        iptables -I FORWARD -i \"$BR\" -o opdbus -j ACCEPT\n    iptables -C FORWARD -i opdbus -o \"$BR\" -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null || \\\n        iptables -I FORWARD -i opdbus -o \"$BR\" -j ACCEPT\n}\n\ncheck_socket\nensure_bridge\nremove_veth_ports\nset_gateway_ip\nset_forwarding\n\necho \"ovsbr0-init: $BR ready (datapath_type=$EXPECTED_DATAPATH fail_mode=$EXPECTED_FAIL_MODE gw=$GW_ADDR)\"\n#!/bin/execlineb -P\nforeground { sh /etc/s6/sv/ovsbr0-static/shell_up }\nexit 0\n#!/bin/execlineb -P\nforeground { sh /etc/s6/sv/ovsbr0-init/shell_up }\nexit 0\n"}}
